screen.reason: The row is carbon-free YPd4B. The search lead is a 2026 ML/DFT prediction paper, which is theory. screen.reason: The row is 71.4 at.% Cd / 28.6 at.% Mg, inside the hcp Cd-Mg solid solution. Claeson, Munkby and Wingbro (Phys. Scr. 7, 80, 1973) measured Tc for several Cd-Mg compositions. Their abstract, read via OpenAlex and the IOP landing page (the PDF is paywalled), says Tc decreases rapidly with Mg and only drops below 30 mK at 50 at.% Mg, with no relevant change between quenched and annealed samples. The table's superconducting rows at 70 at.% Cd (0.105 K) and 75 at.% Cd (0.16 K) fit that smooth trend, so this composition would be expected to superconduct at about 0.1-0.15 K. The 3 zero reports may come from measurements that did not cool below about 0.3-1 K. The full text is needed for the sample list: 70 at.% Cd is 1.4 at.% away, but 75 at.% Cd is 3.6 at.% away, so the bracket rule needs an intermediate sample or a stated 71.4 at.% sample.
screen.best_lead_title: Superconductivity of Cadmium-Magnesium Alloys (Claeson, Munkby, Wingbro, Phys. Scr. 7, 80, 1973)
other_leads: 10.1016/0375-9601(72)91065-1 (Mota, Brewster, Wang 1972, Mg-Cd system Tc; paywalled, no abstract)

reader_a.at_pct_check: Row is Cd 71.4 at.%, Mg 28.6 at.% (Cd5Mg2, equivalently Mg_x Cd_(1-x) with x = 0.286). None of the three abstracts I read gives a Tc at any composition near this one. Claeson et al. 1973 give only 'at 50 at.% Mg less than 30 mK', 21.4 at.% away. Bucher et al. 1972 give a subsidiary Tc maximum at x = 0.20 (20 at.% Mg) but no Tc value, and 20 at.% is 8.6 at.% away. Mota et al. 1972 give only an extrapolated Tc for pure Mg (71.4 at.% away). So the STATED route (within 0.15 at.%) is not met. The BRACKETED route (measured samples within 2 at.% on each side, i.e. somewhere in 26.6 to 28.6 and 28.6 to 30.6 at.% Mg, all superconducting) cannot be checked without the papers' tables or figures.
reader_a.phase_or_sample: Claeson et al. 1973 abstract: bulk Cd-Mg alloys, 'quenched from above the ordering temperature of an intermediate ordered alloy or annealed below that temperature'. The abstract gives no sample list and no phase purity. Bucher et al. 1972 abstract: Mg_xCd_(1-x) alloy series across the system, with an anomaly at x = 0.20 discussed in terms of ordering. No sample list.

reader_a.quote: T c decreases rapidly with increasing Mg content, and is already at 50 at.% Mg less than 30 mK.
reader_a.evidence_note: I read three primary sources for Cd-Mg superconductivity, all at abstract level only. (1) Claeson, Munkby and Wingbro, Phys. Scr. 7, 80 (1973), DOI 10.1088/0031-8949/7/1-2/011: Tc measured for 'several Cd-Mg compositions'. Tc falls rapidly with Mg and is below 30 mK at 50 at.% Mg. No Tc is given for a specific composition other than that bound. (2) Bucher, Heine, Andres, Maita and Cooper, Phys. Rev. B 6, 103 (1972), DOI 10.1103/PhysRevB.6.103 (SciSpace record): on the Cd-rich side Tc drops rapidly with Mg, with a subsidiary Tc maximum at x = 0.20 in Mg_xCd_(1-x). No Tc values are in the abstract. (3) Mota, Brewster and Wang, Phys. Lett. A 41, 99 (1972), DOI 10.1016/0375-9601(72)91065-1 (ScienceDirect abstract page): reports Tc measurements for the Mg-Cd system, with an extrapolated Tc of 0.5 mK for pure Mg. No compositions or Tc values are in the abstract. These abstracts suggest that Cd-rich alloys near 28.6 at.% Mg could be superconducting at around 0.1 K or below. But no source I opened states a Tc for this composition or for bracketing samples.
reader_a.reason_if_not: The deciding data (sample compositions and Tc values) are in the full-text tables and figures of paywalled papers (IOP Physica Scripta 1973, APS Phys. Rev. B 1972, Elsevier Phys. Lett. A 1972). I could not open them from here: the IOP 'bronze' PDF link returned the subscription page. No abstract states a Tc at 28.6 at.% Mg (within 0.15 at.%), or Tc values for samples within 2 at.% on each side. A Tc cannot be taken from the table's neighbouring rows (Cd0.70Mg0.30 and Cd0.75Mg0.25), which are not evidence. Even if those two compositions were measured superconducting samples in one single-phase series, the Mg-poor side (25.0 at.%) is 3.6 at.% away, outside the 2 at.% bracket limit. In addition, the series spans ordered intermediate phases (Bucher's ordering anomaly near x = 0.20, and the intermediate ordered alloy mentioned in the Claeson et al. abstract), so a single-phase series would need to be shown.
leads_for_library: Claeson T., Munkby L., Wingbro T., 'Superconductivity of Cadmium-Magnesium Alloys', Phys. Scr. 7, 80-83 (1973), DOI 10.1088/0031-8949/7/1-2/011: look for the table or figure of Tc against at.% Mg. Is there a sample at or near 28.6 at.% Mg (Cd5Mg2, Mg0.4Cd), and is it superconducting or a null with its lowest temperature? Check samples between 26.6 and 30.6 at.% Mg and their phase (ordered or disordered).

Bucher E., Heine V., Andres K., Maita J. P., Cooper A. S., 'Superconductivity and electronic properties of Mg-Cd and some hcp Mg alloys', Phys. Rev. B 6, 103 (1972), DOI 10.1103/PhysRevB.6.103: the table or figure of Tc against x in Mg_xCd_(1-x). Check for x between 0.266 and 0.306.

Mota A. C., Brewster P., Wang R., 'Superconductivity in the Mg-Cd system: Extrapolated Tc for pure magnesium', Phys. Lett. A 41, 99-101 (1972), DOI 10.1016/0375-9601(72)91065-1: the Tc against composition data.
Claeson T., 'Superconductivity of Magnesium-based Alloys', Phys. Scr. 9 (1974), DOI 10.1088/0031-8949/9/6/011: a comparison that may re-tabulate the Cd-Mg Tc values.

The quote is copied from pdftotext output of the arXiv PDF (subscript rendering may differ slightly from the typeset page).
reader_b.leads_for_library: Published version: Lv et al., Phys. Rev. B 102, 064507 (2020), doi:10.1103/PhysRevB.102.064507, Figs. 2-4. Original discovery report cited as ref. 18: J. P. Remeika, A. S. Cooper, Z. Fisk, D. C. Johnston, 'Superconductivity of single-crystal NbGe2', J. Less-Common Met. 62, 211-213 (1978), doi:10.1016/0022-5088(78)90033-4 (Crossref match; not opened here).

refutation_attempts: Source re-read: downloaded arXiv:2008.10841v1 (8 pages) myself from arxiv.org and read it with pdftotext. Lv et al. text p.3: ZFC/FC dc susceptibility at 20 Oe, 'Tconset = 2.0 K', ZFC volume fraction 'slightly exceeds 100%'. Resistive onset 2.1 K (Fig. 3(a) inset), RRR up to 970. Specific heat at zero field (Fig. 4(a)), p.4: 'A jump around Tc = 2.0 K, in agreement with the observations in the magnetic susceptibility and resistivity, confirms the bulk superconductivity in NbGe2.' Both readers' citations, page and figure numbers match what I read.

Arithmetic: NbGe2 gives Nb 1/3 = 0.33333 and Ge 2/3 = 0.66667. Row: Nb 0.333, Ge 0.667. Differences 0.00033 on each element (0.033 at.%), inside the 0.0015 (0.15 at.%) limit. The paper's composition is the stoichiometric starting ratio and the refined structure (Table I: Nb on 3d, Ge on 6j, a 1:2 ratio); no EDX analysis is reported. The 1978 paper's arc-melted sample was also at nominal NbGe2.

Bulk or film: Lv et al. measured mm-sized single crystals (1 x 1 x 1 mm3 hexagonal pyramids) grown by iodine vapour transport, and the specific-heat jump is a bulk thermodynamic signal. Not a film or nanostructure. Later work on microstructured devices and FIB-irradiated surfaces (Li et al. 2025, Bai et al. 2024) is not used here.
Pressure: no pressure cell or applied pressure appears anywhere in the Experimental details (PPMS, MPMS3 with 3He insert). The text never mentions 'pressure'. Ambient.

Phase purity and impurity check: powder XRD of ground crystals: 'All the patterns can be well indexed with the hexagonal structure' P6222 (Rwp 14.8%). The only impurity the authors mention is a possible 'non-superconducting impurity phase' as one explanation for a small low-T specific-heat deviation. The 2.0 K transition does not match any neighbouring superconducting phase: free Nb is about 9 K, A15 Nb3Ge is 6 K or more, and Nb5Ge3 is 0.30 K (Claeson et al. 1977 abstract, seen in search). Ge is not superconducting at ambient pressure. A transition with near-full shielding and a specific-heat jump at 2.0 K belongs to the main NbGe2 phase. Remeika et al. 1978 isolated the crystals, crushed them, X-rayed them as NbGe2, and found Tc onset 2.1 K.

Independent corroboration I opened: (a) Remeika, Cooper, Fisk, Johnston, J. Less-Common Met. 62, 211 (1978), DOI 10.1016/0022-5088(78)90033-4. I read the full text from the eScholarship CC-BY copy (one Firecrawl scrape, 4 pages). Arc-melted NbGe2 annealed at 950 C for one week had 'Tc = 2.09 +/- 0.02 K'. A single crystal had a resistive Tc of 2.23 +/- 0.03 K. (b) Zhang et al., PRB 103, 214508 (2021), arXiv:2106.14419 (opened): single crystals with Tc = 2.0-2.1 K, plus a specific-heat jump and resistive drop. (c) Jiao et al., PRB 110, 214516 (2024), arXiv:2412.08994 (opened): polycrystalline NbGe2 made by solid-state reaction, Tc = 2.0-2.1 K, measured by muSR. Other groups' abstracts seen in search also report superconductivity near 2 K: Emmanouilidou et al. PRB 102, 235144 (2020) and Yao et al. PRMaterials 9, 034803 (2025).

Where the table's zero likely comes from: the 1978 Remeika paper says 'Hardy and Hulm [5] found the C40 compound NbGe2 to be normal to 1.2 K'. Ref. 5 is G. F. Hardy and J. K. Hulm, Phys. Rev. 93, 1004 (1954), DOI 10.1103/PhysRev.93.1004 (Crossref match). This 1954 null is the most likely source of the SuperCon zero entries. I did not open the 1954 paper itself (APS, paywalled); I know it only through Remeika's citation. The 1978 authors re-measured an arc-melted bulk NbGe2 sample of the same nominal composition and found Tc = 2.09 K. Every later bulk measurement I found (single crystals and polycrystals, from several groups) also finds Tc = 2.0-2.1 K. The 1954 null is therefore an early outlier, superseded by direct re-measurement. It is not an unresolved contradiction.

Later corrections or retractions: none found. Crossref lists no retraction for 10.1103/PhysRevB.102.064507 (the tool notes that this check is not conclusive). The paper has been cited about 35-38 times, and the citing NbGe2 papers I saw all treat it as a superconductor at about 2 K.

The high Tc claims are not relevant here. The '16 K' superconductivity in sputtered Nb-Ge films (Ghosh and Douglass 1976; Knoedler and Douglass 1979) is film work, and a web snippet attributes it to contamination. It is not used. The row is corrected with the about 2 K bulk value only.

Quote (p.4): 'A jump around Tc = 2.0 K, in agreement with the observations in the magnetic susceptibility and resistivity, confirms the bulk superconductivity in NbGe2.' sceptic.verifier_reason: I re-read the cited paper myself and found the deciding statements where both readers placed them. Bulk single-crystal NbGe2 shows a diamagnetic onset at 2.0 K with ZFC shielding above 100%, a resistive onset at 2.1 K and a zero-field specific-heat jump at 2.0 K that the authors say confirms bulk superconductivity. The measurements are at ambient pressure, and the sample indexes as single-phase C40 NbGe2. The stoichiometric formula lies 0.033 at.% from the row on each element, inside the 0.15 at.% limit. The 2.0 K transition cannot come from free Nb (about 9 K), Nb3Ge (6 K or more), Nb5Ge3 (0.3 K) or Ge. I found one contrary report: Hardy and Hulm (Phys. Rev. 93, 1004, 1954) reported NbGe2 'normal to 1.2 K'. This is probably where the SuperCon zero comes from. I could not open the 1954 paper and know it only through the 1978 paper's citation. The 1978 discovery paper, which I read, re-measured an arc-melted NbGe2 sample of the same nominal composition and found Tc = 2.09 K. At least three further bulk studies I opened, on single crystals and on polycrystals, also report Tc = 2.0-2.1 K. I found no correction or retraction. The old null is superseded, so it does not give me a reason of substance to doubt that bulk NbGe2 superconducts at ambient pressure near 2 K. The readers' STATED confirmation stands, and the label should be corrected with Tc = 2.0 K.

refutation_attempts: Re-read the readers' source myself (arXiv:0905.2115 v1). Table I: LT098, nominal FeSe0.98, Tc 8.21 K, main phase FeSe0.975(3) (P4/nmm) 98.31 molar %, Fe 0.57 %, hexagonal FeSe 1.12 %. Abstract and conclusions: superconducting phase FeSe0.974+-0.005, Tc about 8 K. Bulk polycrystalline, magnetization in PPMS/MPMS, no pressure applied. The readers' transcription is accurate.

Arithmetic. Row Fe/Se = 1.0284 (FeSe0.9724). FeSe0.974: Fe 0.50659 (-0.041 at.%); FeSe0.975: Fe 0.50633 (-0.067 at.%); both inside 0.15 at.%. But the match rests only on the refined Se occupancy of the main phase. The sample's nominal composition FeSe0.98 is Fe 0.50505 (-0.195 at.%, outside). The paper's own second refinement of LT098 at lambda = 1.155 A gave occupancy 0.980(3), Fe 0.50505 (-0.195 at.%, outside). The paper's stated systematic error (< 0.005 in x) is about 0.13 at.%, nearly the whole tolerance. So whether the superconducting phase lies within 0.15 at.% of the row depends on a refinement whose stated uncertainty is about as large as the tolerance itself.

Bulk/pressure/phase. Pomjakushina's samples are bulk, at ambient pressure, and the superconductivity belongs to the main tetragonal phase (not Fe, and not hexagonal FeSe, which McQueen reports as non-superconducting to 0.6 K). No objection on these grounds.

Contrary report at the same composition, found and read in full: McQueen et al., PRB 79, 014522 (2009). Bulk beta-Fe1+dSe made from Fe pieces and Se shot under oxygen exclusion, quenched. Fe1.03Se (Fe 0.50739, +0.039 at.% from the row, inside the tolerance) shows no superconductivity to 0.6 K 'irrespective of the synthesis temperature'. They checked this by DC magnetization (Fig. 2b), specific heat (Fig. 4), and resistivity (Fig. 5: 'no superconductivity'). The paper reads the loss as an intrinsic change in defect chemistry of the beta phase (c/a about 1.461), not as an impurity effect.

Second contrary report by the same group: McQueen et al., PRL 103, 057002 (2009) (arXiv:0905.1065). It studies Fe1.03Se, refined with the structural formula FeSe0.97, and reports 'no Tc > 0.5 K'. It also finds that Fe1.03Se, unlike superconducting Fe1.01Se, stays tetragonal at low temperature. Two independent publications reporting a null at this composition match the table's '2 zero reports'. The table's same-system neighbours Fe:0.502 (Fe1.01Se) and Fe:0.505 (Fe1.02Se) are superconducting and also follow McQueen's nominal-composition series. So the zero label is very probably a faithful transcription of McQueen's Fe1.03Se, not a data error.

Is the McQueen null later corrected or retracted? FastTrack verify_reference found no retraction flag on either DOI. Williams, McQueen and Cava, SSC 149, 1507 (2009) (read in full) restates the 'extreme sensitivity of superconductivity to small deviations from stoichiometry' and puts the superconductor at Fe1.01Se. The 2016 review by Rossler et al. (secondary) cites both results side by side: McQueen's 'Fe1.03Se is not a superconductor at all' and Pomjakushina's FeSe0.974 (about Fe1.027Se). It then cites Koz et al., who find the beta-FeSe stability range narrows to nominal Fe1.00Se-Fe1.01Se. I found no paper that withdraws the Fe1.03Se null. Later work places the superconducting phase nearer Fe1.00-1.01Se, which makes the Fe-rich refined occupancy in Pomjakushina the weaker of the two composition assignments.

Different composition definitions. McQueen labels samples by starting composition, and its NPD fixes the beta-phase composition only to about +-0.02 in delta (about +-0.5 at.%). Pomjakushina labels the phase by refined Se occupancy, and its two wavelengths differ by 0.005 (0.13 at.%). Neither paper determines the phase composition to 0.15 at.%. On the evidence available, the literature conflicts at exactly this composition, and the conflict is not resolved in favour of superconductivity.

sceptic.verifier_reason: The readers transcribed Pomjakushina et al. (PRB 80, 024517) correctly. Its superconducting tetragonal phase has a refined composition of FeSe0.974-0.975, within 0.067 at.% of the row, in bulk samples at ambient pressure with Tc of about 8.2 K. But the same composition, Fe1.03Se (0.039 at.% from the row), is reported as a bulk, ambient-pressure non-superconductor by McQueen et al. in two verified, unretracted papers. PRB 79, 014522 reports no superconductivity to 0.6 K in magnetization, specific heat and resistivity, 'irrespective of the synthesis temperature'. PRL 103, 057002 reports no Tc above 0.5 K. These are almost certainly the table's two zero reports, so the label is a faithful record of a primary null, not a transcription error. Pomjakushina's match rests entirely on a refined Se occupancy. Their own shorter-wavelength refinement of the same sample (0.980) and their stated systematic error (about 0.13 at.%) put it at or beyond the 0.15 at.% limit. Later work (Williams et al. 2009; Koz et al. as cited in the 2016 review) places the superconducting beta phase near Fe1.00-1.01Se, not Fe1.027Se. Pomjakushina et al. themselves say their result disagrees with McQueen's. So a primary, peer-reviewed null at this exact composition is a reason of substance to doubt that a bulk sample of this composition superconducts. Under the rule, doubt means do_not_apply. The label 'not a superconductor' should stay. This row is better recorded as a documented literature conflict, with McQueen's Fe1.03Se null as the supporting source.

Fei's x = 0.2 sample (Ir 26.67, Pt 6.67, Te 66.67 at.%) and x = 0.3 sample (Ir 23.33, Pt 10.00, Te 66.67 at.%) each differ from the row by 1.67 at.% in Ir and Pt and 0.00 in Te. The readers' bracket arithmetic holds, within the 2 at.% limit on both sides.

Composition basis: Fei's x values are nominal. The Methods give the flux charge as Ir:Pt:Te = 0.18(1-x):0.18x:0.82, and the EDS in Fig. 2b inset is qualitative only (no measured compositions). Fu et al. show that nominal and measured x can differ: their nominal x = 0.1 crystal measured Te 66.85, Ir 29.20, Pt 3.94 at.% by EDX (Pt/(Ir+Pt) = 0.119). Different labs' x scales are therefore not exactly comparable.
Bulk and pressure: Fei's samples are mm-sized flux-grown single crystals, measured by resistance in a dilution refrigerator with no applied pressure described. Bulk sample at ambient pressure: yes.

Phase and impurity: Fei states the pure 1T (P-3m1) phase from powder XRD (pattern shown only for x = 0.4) and no structural transition in R(T) for x = 0.1-0.4. Superconductivity rests on resistance alone (Fig. 5a, zero resistance below about 0.6 K for x = 0.2 and about 0.13 K for x = 0.3, plus Bc2(T) in Fig. 5b). There is no magnetization or specific heat. Elemental Ir (Tc about 0.11 K) is the only plausible elemental superconductor in this system; the monotonic Tc trend argues against it, but bulk superconductivity of the x = 0.3 crystal is not shown thermodynamically.

Where the bracket puts Tc: Fei's own phase-diagram curve (Fig. 5c), read from pixels at 400 dpi, gives 0.64 K at x = 0.2 and 0.15 K at x = 0.3 (matching the labelled values) and about 0.40 K at x = 0.25. Linear interpolation also gives 0.40 K.

Contrary report for the same composition (found by this sceptic, not by either reader): Fu et al. grew Te-flux single crystals from arc-melted Ir1-xPtx alloys with x = 0.05, 0.1, 0.25 and 0.5. EDX on several crystals and areas was 'consistent with the corresponding nominal ones'. They measured resistivity in a He-3 system and report no superconductivity above 0.3 K for x = 0.25 (Fig. 2a: the x = 0.25 trace is flat from the lowest plotted temperature to 8 K). This is a direct measurement at the row's exact composition (0.00 at.% from the row). It contradicts the about 0.40 K that Fei's bracket and curve imply for x = 0.25.

Likely origin of the table's zeros: Pyon et al. 2012 made polycrystals with 0 <= x <= 0.25 and saw 'No trace of superconductivity ... for x >= 0.10 down to 2.0 K'. Fu et al. 2019 give the x = 0.25 null to 0.3 K. The task reports two zero reports for this row. The table also holds Ir:0.293;Pt:0.040;Te:0.667 as a superconductor (Tc 1.92 K), which matches Fu's EDX composition of their nominal x = 0.1 crystal (Ir 29.20, Pt 3.94, Te 66.85 at.%). So the database probably took Fu's measurements, including the x = 0.25 null, but I have not seen the database record.

Later corrections and the published version: arXiv has only v1 of 1711.10909. The published Adv. Mater. version (19 authors, retitled) could not be read: Wiley Scholar Gateway's free allowance is used up. Its abstract states superconductivity 'persists when the Fermi level aligns with the Dirac points', which in the preprint is the x = 0.3 sample. The 2020 APL Mater. paper (overlapping authors, crystals from the Adv. Mater. work) repeats x = 0.2 (about 0.65 K), x = 0.3 (about 0.15 K), and no superconductivity for x = 0.4 down to 400 mK. No erratum or retraction was found; FastTrack verify_reference flagged no retraction.

sceptic.evidence_note: Not applied, so no evidence row is given. For the record, the readers' source is Fei et al., Adv. Mater. 30, 1801556 (2018), DOI 10.1002/adma.201801556 (verified with Crossref by FastTrack), read as arXiv:1711.10909v1. Fig. 5a shows R(T) for nominal x = 0.1, 0.2 and 0.3 with Tc = 1.7, 0.65 and 0.15 K. x = 0.25 itself was not measured.
sceptic.verifier_reason: The readers' arithmetic and reading of Fei et al. are correct. Nominal Ir0.8Pt0.2Te2 (Tc 0.65 K) and Ir0.7Pt0.3Te2 (Tc 0.15 K) are each 1.67 at.% from the row and both reach zero resistance, so the BRACKETED route is met on paper. I still found a reason of substance to doubt that Ir0.75Pt0.25Te2 superconducts, which neither reader found. Fu et al. (Chin. Phys. B 28, 037103 (2019); arXiv:1712.02500, read in full) measured flux-grown single crystals at exactly x = 0.25, with EDX stated consistent with nominal. In a He-3 cryostat they saw no superconductivity above 0.3 K (Fig. 2a), at ambient pressure. The bracket, by linear interpolation or from Fei's own Fig. 5c curve (about 0.40 K at x = 0.25 by pixel reading), predicts a Tc above that limit. So the only direct measurement of this composition contradicts what the bracket implies. A Tc below 0.3 K is not excluded, but no paper shows it, and there is then no defensible Tc value to enter. Three things add to the doubt. Fei's x values are nominal flux-charge ratios with no quantitative EDS, and Fu's data show nominal and measured x differing by about 0.02 between labs. Fei's superconductivity at x = 0.2-0.3 rests on resistance alone, with no magnetization or specific heat. And the existing zero label likely comes from real measurements at this exact composition (Fu to 0.3 K; Pyon et al. to 2.0 K). Under the owner's rule, when in doubt, do not apply. The row should stay 'not a superconductor' until a measurement on x = 0.25 below 0.3 K, or bulk evidence on a composition-checked bracketing series, settles it.

refutation_attempts: Source re-read: I opened the publisher landing page https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/BF00682295 (one Firecrawl scrape, 1 credit) and the SciSpace record of the same paper. Both carry the identical abstract, which states 'NbSi2 and TaSi2 are found to be superconductors at 0.130K and 0.353K respectively.' The full text is paywalled ('preview of subscription content'), so the figure or table with the transition was not seen.

Composition arithmetic: NbSi2 gives Nb = 1/3 = 0.33333 and Si = 2/3 = 0.66667. Row: Nb 0.333, Si 0.667. Differences 0.00033 and 0.00033 (0.033 at.% each), below the 0.0015 (0.15 at.%) STATED limit. The readers' arithmetic holds.

Bulk or film: the JLTP abstract reports low-temperature specific heat (a bulk thermodynamic measurement) and does not itself name the sample form. A same-group abstract I opened (Gottlieb, Balkashin, Jansen, Laborde, Madar, MRS Proc. 320, 485, 1993, DOI 10.1557/PROC-320-485) describes the VSi2, NbSi2 and TaSi2 samples as 'high quality single crystals' and says the low-temperature specific heat was 'measured on the same samples'. The JLTP reference list (read on the Springer page) cites the group's single-crystal TaSi2 paper (Phys. Rev. B 45, 4803, 1992). Nothing points to a film or nanostructure.

Pressure: nothing in the abstract mentions applied pressure; it is a standard calorimetry study. The later same-group abstract (Keller, Laborde, Gottlieb, Madar, MRS Proc. 402, 619, 1995, DOI 10.1557/PROC-402-619) quotes 'TaSi2, and NbSi2 are superconductors below 353 mK and 130 mK respectively' as the reference values and reports pressure effects on TaSi2 separately, consistent with 0.130 K being the ambient-pressure Tc.

Phase purity and impurity check: the authors attribute the transition to NbSi2 itself ('NbSi2 ... found to be superconductors'). The Nb-rich impurity routes I could check point to much higher Tc: Deardorff et al., J. Less-Common Met. (1969), abstract opened, find Nb-Si ingots superconducting near 7.5 K up to 37.5 at.% Si, so an Nb-rich second phase would show near 7.5 K, not at 0.13 K. I found no Nb-Si phase reported to superconduct near 0.13 K other than NbSi2. Phase purity of the specimen is not stated in the abstract (full text not read).

Contrary reports and corrections: I searched for measurements of NbSi2 that found no superconductivity, and for later corrections. None was found below 0.13 K. Hardy and Hulm, Phys. Rev. 93, 1004 (1954), DOI 10.1103/PhysRev.93.1004 (abstract opened) tested about eighty transition-metal compounds including silicides only down to 1.20 K, and NbSi2 is not among the eleven new superconductors listed. That is a plausible origin of a table zero, but it does not conflict with Tc = 0.13 K. Knoedler and Douglass, J. Low Temp. Phys. 37, 189 (1979), DOI 10.1007/BF00114067 (abstract opened) report NbSi2 superconducting with Tc = 2.9 K in a study centred on sputtered films. That is inconsistent with 0.13 K and is probably a film or second-phase effect, but it is a positive report, not a null. The 20 most-cited works citing the 1993 paper (FastTrack get_citations) include no contrary report. Garcia et al., arXiv 2012.09207 (read via alphaXiv) states that NbGe2 and NbSi2 'exhibit superconducting transitions at low temperatures'.

Later NbSi2 crystal studies: Sato et al., arXiv 2311.11341 (read via alphaXiv) measured NbSi2 Czochralski crystals by PPMS resistivity and thermopower and makes no statement about superconductivity or its absence. Lv et al., arXiv 2008.10841 (NbGe2, read via alphaXiv) does not mention NbSi2 superconductivity. The Onuki et al. abstract (J. Phys. Soc. Jpn. 83, 061018, 2014, dHvA on TaSi2, NbSi2 and VSi2) makes no statement about superconductivity.

sceptic.verifier_reason: I re-read the deciding statement myself on the publisher's page and in SciSpace: the abstract of Lasjaunias et al., J. Low Temp. Phys. 92, 335 (1993), DOI 10.1007/BF00682295 (verified with Crossref), states that NbSi2 in the C40 structure is a superconductor at 0.130 K, from low-temperature specific heat. NbSi2 matches the row within 0.033 at.% on each element. The measurement is calorimetric (bulk), and a same-group abstract places it on high-quality single crystals. No pressure is involved. No Nb-Si impurity phase I could check superconducts near 0.13 K (Nb-rich phases near 7.5 K), and the authors attribute the transition to NbSi2. The only null-type report I found (Hardy and Hulm 1954) stopped at 1.20 K, above the reported Tc. The other positive report (Knoedler and Douglass 1979, 2.9 K) differs in Tc but does not say NbSi2 is non-superconducting. The remaining weaknesses are that the full text was not read, so the Tc definition and specimen phase purity are unseen; the owner's option B does not allow refusing on those grounds alone. I found no reason of substance to doubt that bulk NbSi2 at ambient pressure superconducts near 0.13 K, so the 'not a superconductor' label should be corrected.

refutation_attempts: Re-read the source myself: downloaded arXiv:1512.01245v3 (11 pages; the OA copy that FastTrack get_paper links to DOI 10.1103/PhysRevB.93.094522). Read the abstract, Sec. II (synthesis), Sec. III (structure, Table I), Sec. IV (susceptibility, heat capacity, transport), the pressure paragraph (Fig. 9) and the conclusions with pdftotext, and viewed page 6 (Figs. 4 and 5) as an image. The deciding statements are as both readers report them.

Composition arithmetic: the paper's formula is FeS, so Fe = 1/2 = 0.5000 and S = 1/2 = 0.5000. The row is Fe 0.500, S 0.500. The difference is 0.0000 on both elements, inside the 0.0015 limit. Table I caption: 'In the FeS samples, we found full occupancy for the iron and sulfur sites' (Rietveld fit of ground single crystals). Weak point: the paper gives no bulk chemical analysis. Surface EDS showed up to 9% total alkali (K, Na), which the authors attribute to the surface because c = 5.03440(9) A matches earlier FeS reports. Intercalated FeS phases have a much larger c, so the measured c argues against bulk intercalation.

Bulk vs film: single crystals 3-8 mm across, about 0.1 mm thick (precursor dimensions; FeS forms crystal-to-crystal). ZFC shielding 60-90% without demagnetisation correction. A specific-heat anomaly at 3.9 K, suppressed by 3 T, is shown in Fig. 4, which I viewed: the 0 T C/T curve rises above the 3 T curve below the arrow marked T = 3.9 K. Not a film or nanostructure.

Pressure: the susceptibility (Fig. 3), heat capacity (Fig. 4) and transport (Fig. 5) data were taken in MPMS/PPMS without a pressure cell. The piston-cylinder cell is used only for the separate Fig. 9 series, where Tc falls with pressure. The published abstract (FastTrack get_paper) says FeS shows superconductivity 'at ambient pressure'.

Impurity phase: the superconducting phase is tetragonal FeS itself (P4/nmm, a = 3.6286(5) A, c = 5.03440(9) A). The precursor KxFe2-yS2 is non-superconducting (Lei et al., cited; Fig. S1). Fe, Na2S, NaOH, greigite Fe3S4 and pyrrhotite are not superconductors at 4 K, so no known superconducting impurity could carry a 3.5-3.9 K transition with 60-90% shielding and a specific-heat anomaly.

Independent replication of the same composition (abstracts read via OpenAlex/FastTrack): Lai et al., JACS 137, 10148 (2015), DOI 10.1021/jacs.5b06687, superconductivity at 5 K in hydrothermal tetragonal FeS, stoichiometry stressed. Terashima et al., PRB 94, 100503 (2016), DOI 10.1103/PhysRevB.94.100503, Tc = 4.1 K in FeS. Holenstein et al., PRB 93, 140506(R) (2016), DOI 10.1103/PhysRevB.93.140506, muSR shows bulk superconductivity. Kirschner et al., PRB 94, 134509 (2016), DOI 10.1103/PhysRevB.94.134509, muSR consistent. Pachmayr et al., Chem. Commun. (2016), DOI 10.1039/c5cc07739g, hydrothermal tetragonal FeS superconducting. Zhang et al., npj Quantum Mater. (2017), DOI 10.1038/s41535-017-0050-7, FeS Tc about 4.5 K at ambient pressure.

Contrary reports: searched FastTrack ('evidence for non-metallic behaviour in tetragonal FeS'; 'absence of superconductivity tetragonal FeS mackinawite magnetism'; 'troilite hexagonal FeS low temperature resistivity superconductivity search'; 'non-superconducting tetragonal FeS iron vacancies sulfur excess suppression superconductivity') and the arXiv listing for 'tetragonal FeS mackinawite'. Found the two NIMS papers by Denholme et al. (2014). I read one in full (arXiv:1410.2685 = STAM 15, 055007). Its sample is Fe1.08S by EDX (Fe:S = 0.52:0.48), i.e. Fe 51.9 at.% vs the row's 50.0 at.%, about 1.9 at.% away, outside 0.15 at.%. It was measured to 2 K without superconductivity. It is not a null for exact FeS. Borg et al. (p. 9) attribute the earlier non-metallic, non-superconducting results to surface oxidation and Fe3S4 impurity. Borg also states that their own samples made without excess Fe powder were not superconducting, so superconductivity is sample-dependent but present in the stoichiometric phase.

Later corrections or retraction: FastTrack get_paper and Crossref (verify_reference) show no retraction flag for 10.1103/PhysRevB.93.094522. The paper has 85 citations through 2026, and the later literature (two-dome pressure studies, Cr doping 2025, Se doping 2022) treats FeS as an established ambient-pressure superconductor. Found no paper withdrawing the superconductivity.

Polymorph check: superconductivity belongs to the metastable tetragonal (mackinawite) polymorph. Hexagonal troilite FeS, the stable polymorph at the same composition, is not reported as a superconductor in what I found. The owner's rule decides by composition, and a bulk, ambient-pressure FeS phase at exactly this composition superconducts, so the polymorph is a caveat to record, not a refutation.

DOI check: FastTrack verify_reference on 10.1103/PhysRevB.93.094522 shows it registered with Crossref: Phys. Rev. B 93(9), 094522 (2016), Borg, Zhou, Eckberg, Campbell, Saha, Paglione, Rodriguez. Title matches the arXiv copy.

sceptic.verifier_reason: I re-read Borg et al. (PRB 93, 094522; arXiv:1512.01245v3) in full and tried to refute both readers on composition, form, pressure, phase and contrary reports. None of these attempts succeeded. The paper's formula FeS matches the row exactly (0.0000 difference), backed by a Rietveld refinement with full Fe and S occupancy. The samples are bulk single crystals measured without applied pressure. Superconductivity is carried by the FeS phase itself, shown by 60-90% ZFC shielding and a specific-heat anomaly at 3.9 K that 3 T suppresses, which I saw in Fig. 4. The only contrary measurements I found are the 2014 NIMS reports by Denholme et al. One is read in full: its sample is Fe1.08S (Fe:S = 0.52:0.48, about 1.9 at.% Fe-rich), measured to 2 K. It falls outside the 0.15 at.% window, and later work explains it by off-stoichiometry, oxidation and Fe3S4 impurity. Several independent groups have since confirmed bulk superconductivity in tetragonal FeS at 4-5 K, including muSR, and I found no retraction or correction. The DOI is registered with Crossref and matches. Caveats that do not refute the label: the superconductor is the metastable tetragonal polymorph, not hexagonal troilite, and the stoichiometry comes from site occupancy rather than chemical analysis. Under the owner's composition-based rule, the 'not a superconductor' label for Fe:0.500;S:0.500 is wrong. Apply.

Claeson 1974 (abstract, Physica Scripta 9, 353): compares Tc in compounds and intermediate phases of Mg with Al, Cd, Hg, In, Zn or Cu-Si and says Tc drops rapidly once Mg exceeds about 50 at.%; it names no individual Hg-Mg compound and gives no Tc. So what I read contains no Tc and no null statement for the row's composition. The two nearest compounds named as superconducting are separate stoichiometric compounds 4.73 and 3.60 at.% away, not samples of one single-phase series, so the bracketed route does not apply either.

reader_a.tc_criterion: not applicable: no transition was observed

reader_a.measurement_method: Electrical resistivity versus temperature on two single crystals, contacts made with gold wires and silver paste; PPMS down to 2 K, dilution refrigerator down to 12 mK. No magnetisation or specific-heat test for superconductivity is reported.
reader_a.synthesis_conditions: Single crystals 'grown using the flux method'. The main text gives no flux, temperatures or times.
reader_a.quote: The resistivity decreases monotonically from 300 K and forms a plateau at low temperatures down to 12 mK, exhibiting a typical metallic behaviour. In contrast to a previous report of superconductivity at 64 mK [39], our resistivity data show no sign of superconductivity.
reader_a.evidence_note: Two primary papers disagree on this exact composition, and I could open only one of them in full. (1) Tsui et al., Phys. Rev. B 111, L121111 (2025), read in full as arXiv:2503.10130v1: NbAl3 single crystals, resistivity measured down to 12 mK, 'no sign of superconductivity', written explicitly in contrast to the 1977 report (its reference 39). This meets the definition of verified_null. (2) Leyarovski et al., Z. Phys. B 27, 57-60 (1977), DOI 10.1007/bf01315504, read as abstract only (the abstract as carried by the SciSpace index record for that DOI; the full text is closed access and was not read). The abstract says magnetic properties were investigated down to 0.42 K and: 'It has been found that theσ-phase (Nb2Al) and the intermetallic compound NbAl3 are superconductors with superconducting transition temperature 0.74°K and 0.64°K, respectively.' The abstract gives no sample form, preparation, phase analysis or Tc criterion. Note a mismatch: Tsui et al. quote the earlier report as superconductivity at 64 mK, while the 1977 abstract says 0.64 K (640 mK). The 12 mK measurement lies below both values, so the mismatch does not change the reading. Limits of the null: it rests on resistivity only; the main-text Fig. 1(b) plots 0 to 300 K with no low-temperature inset, so the 12 mK statement is textual; the powder diffraction pattern is in a supplement I did not see; I read the arXiv version, not the journal page.
reader_a.reason_if_not: Why this is not 'confirmed': the 1977 abstract does state NbAl3 and a Tc (0.64 K), which on its face is the STATED route under the abstract rule. I refuse on substance, not because it is an abstract. First, the only full text I could open for this composition is a later primary paper that measured single-phase single crystals to 12 mK, about 50 times below the claimed Tc, and found no superconductivity, in explicit contradiction of the 1977 report. Second, the 1977 abstract reports a magnetic measurement only and says nothing about whether the sample was bulk and single-phase, so from what I read an impurity-phase origin of the 0.64 K signal cannot be excluded. The label 'not a superconductor' is therefore supported, not contradicted, by the best source I could read.

B 111, L121111 (Fig. S1, powder x-ray diffraction) and the journal page, to see the low-temperature resistivity data and whether '64 mK' was corrected to 0.64 K. 3. reader_a.evidence_note: Cao et al. (Zhejiang) made a single-phase polycrystalline series EuFe2(As1-xPx)2 including x = 0.35 and 0.40, which bracket the row (x = 0.36) at 0.4 and 1.6 at.%. The authors state superconductivity for 0.2 <= x <= 0.4 (abstract and p. 6) and 'When x >0.45, no sign of SC was detected' (p. 4); Fig. 5 places Tc points at x = 0.35 (about 24 K) and x = 0.40 (about 22 K) inside the SC dome. So the BRACKETED route is met as the rule is written, and the authors call the transitions superconductivity of the phase (attributed to Fe-3d electrons). Weaknesses a sceptic should weigh: (1) the x = 0.35 sample is shown only as a Fig. 5 point, with no resistivity or magnetization curve; (2) the x = 0.40 sample shows only a partial resistive drop (to about 25% of rho(40 K) at about 3 K), followed by a T_M(Eu) anomaly; (3) the paper itself reports no Meissner shielding in low-field M(H) even for x = 0.3 and says 'the resistivity is not really zero', ascribed to weak links or spontaneous vortices; (4) compositions are nominal; (5) single-crystal studies disagree: Jeevan et al., PRB 83, 054511 (2011) abstract says superconductivity is fully suppressed for x >= 0.22, and Zapf et al., PRL 110, 237002 (2013) (arXiv:1305.5672, opened) report 'we do not see any signature of superconductivity in our x=0.35 crystal' and argue the polycrystal anomalies near x = 0.4 are purely magnetic. Cao et al. acknowledge the single-crystal discrepancy and attribute it to Eu deficiency in crystals. Nowik et al., JPCM 23, 065701 (2011) (abstract only, same Zhejiang samples) states 'For 0.2 < x < 0.5, the system becomes superconducting', consistent with Cao et al.

reader_a.evidence_note: Two sets of primary papers disagree about this composition, and I report both. (1) Direct measurement at the exact composition: Jeevan et al., PRB 83, 054511 (arXiv:1011.4481v2, full text read) measured a single crystal with EDX-determined x = 0.26, which matches the row exactly. The authors state 'For larger P concentrations, x >= 0.26, the SC transition is fully suppressed', that the 50 Oe ZFC/FC susceptibility of x = 0.26 shows only the Eu ferromagnetic anomaly at 20 K and 'no sign for a SC phase', and that 'In our single crystals, with x=0.26 and 0.38, we did not observe any such drop in resistivity'. Fig. 2 shows chi(T) for x = 0.26 from about 3 K (read from the figure) to 40 K with no diamagnetism, and the text gives isothermal magnetization at 2 K showing ferromagnetic hysteresis; I record 2 K as the lowest stated temperature. The published abstract (OpenAlex) says superconductivity is fully suppressed for x >= 0.22. Caveat for the auditor: the lower-left panel of Fig. 1 does show the x = 0.26 normalized resistivity falling from about 0.13 near 22 K to about 0.05, with a bump near 17-18 K, without reaching zero; the authors do not call this superconductivity. A later paper from the same group, Zapf et al., PRL 110, 237002 (2013) (arXiv:1305.5672, full text read), measured an x = 0.26 single crystal, plots an open grey resistive Tc,on of about 23 K at x = 0.26 in Fig. 3, and says 'Between the concentrations x ~ 0.12 and x ~ 0.26 the onset of a superconducting transition is found, while fully developed bulk superconductivity occurs in an even narrower regime'. So the exact composition shows at most a partial (filamentary) resistive onset that its authors do not call bulk superconductivity. Tokiwa et al., PRB 86, 220505 (arXiv:1210.5440, full text read) restate that single crystals with x >= 0.26 lack bulk superconductivity and place the upper limit of the dome at x = 0.23. (2) Bracketing polycrystals: Cao et al., JPCM 23, 464204 (arXiv:1105.3255, full text read) made a solid-state polycrystalline series (x = 0 to 1, nominal compositions, 'basically of single phase', minor < 5% Eu2O3/Fe2P in some samples) and report superconductivity for 0.2 <= x <= 0.4; their x = 0.25 (0.4 at.% away) and x = 0.30 (1.6 at.% away) samples both show resistive transitions they call superconducting (onsets about 25 K and 29 K). So the BRACKETED route is formally met by text I read. The same paper notes the x = 0.3 sample shows no Meissner shielding in low-field magnetization and that 'the resistivity is not really zero'. Ren et al., PRL 102, 137002 (arXiv:0811.2390, full text read) report bulk superconductivity in an x = 0.30 polycrystal (resistive midpoint 26 K, ac diamagnetism after subtraction, specific heat anomaly at about 26 K). The Göttingen authors attribute the polycrystal superconductivity at x >= 0.26 to inhomogeneous P content; Cao et al. attribute the narrower single-crystal dome to Eu deficiency. Why I chose verified_null over confirmed: the bracket is an interpolation between nominal compositions 0.4 and 1.6 at.% away, while the exact composition (EDX-checked) was measured directly, in bulk, at ambient pressure, and stated not to superconduct. The row's current label matches that direct measurement.
reader_a.reason_if_not: Not confirmed as a superconductor. No paper I read states superconductivity at x = 0.26 within 0.15 at.% (the nearest stated superconducting samples are polycrystals at x = 0.25 and 0.27 to 0.30, at least 0.4 at.% away in P). The BRACKETED route is formally met by the Cao et al. (2011) polycrystalline series (x = 0.25 and 0.30, both called superconducting), but a direct, EDX-checked single-crystal measurement at exactly x = 0.26 (Jeevan et al. 2011) states no superconductivity down to about 2-3 K, and the same group's later x = 0.26 crystal (Zapf et al. 2013) shows only a resistive onset that is not called bulk superconductivity. If the owner decides that the bracket should override, the sceptic must weigh these contrary reports.

reader_a.synthesis_conditions: Scandium ingot and sulphur powder weighed in a ratio of 1:1.2, melted together on a water-cooled copper hearth under argon; ingots flipped and remelted several times; no anneal reported.
reader_a.quote: The starting materials for the preparation of ScS were scandium ingot, and sulphur powder which were weighed in a ratio of 1:1.2 and melted together on a water-cooled copper hearth under an argon gas atmosphere.
reader_a.evidence_note: Arushi et al. (Phys. Rev. B 106, L020504, 2022; arXiv:2203.16458v1) report bulk superconductivity in a sample they call ScS: 'it exhibits a diamagnetic signal at a superconducting transition temperature of TC,onset = 5.10(5) K', zero resistivity, a specific-heat jump at 4.8(1) K and a Meissner fraction 'close to 100 %'. The paper does not establish the composition of that sample. Its supplement says the elements were weighed in a ratio of 1:1.2, the main text calls the structure 'cubic (NaCl defect)', Table S1 has no occupancies, and no chemical analysis is given. The accepted journal version (STFC ePubs copy, main text only) has the same synthesis sentence and lattice constant and adds no composition data. Context read in this session from abstracts only: Moodenbaugh et al. 1978 say Tc 'was established as a function of composition' for the Sc-S NaCl-structure system and name the superconductor Sc1-xS; the 1974 paper's title names 'ScS1+x'; Tuenge, Laabs and Franzen (J. Chem. Phys. 1976) report that 'a defect scandium monosulfide phase with composition Sc/S=0.8065 vaporizes congruently'. A 1:1.2 charge is Sc/S = 0.833, close to that defect composition. The task table also holds a separate row S:0.501;Sc:0.499 labelled superconductor at 5.37 K. For these reasons I did not treat the name ScS as a composition statement good to 0.15 at.%. If the owner accepts a paper's compound name as its composition, the STATED route would be met by this paper with Tc = 5.1 K (magnetisation onset); that is a judgement for the auditor, and the passage that decides it is the synthesis sentence quoted here.
reader_a.reason_if_not: The only primary paper opened in full reports superconductivity for a sample named ScS whose composition is not shown to be within 0.15 at.% of Sc 50 / S 50: the weighed charge was Sc:S = 1:1.2 (45.45 / 54.55 at.% if molar, 4.55 at.% from the row on each element), the product was not analysed, and the phase is described in the paper as a defect NaCl structure and in the literature it cites as a variable-composition phase whose Tc depends on composition. The papers that measured Tc against composition in the Sc-S system (Moodenbaugh et al. 1974 and 1978) and Narayan and Finnemore 1978 are paywalled and were not read; the two abstracts I could read give no Tc for a stated composition. So neither STATED nor BRACKETED is met by text I read. verified_null is not met either: nothing I read says stoichiometric ScS was measured and did not superconduct.
leads_for_library: A. R. Moodenbaugh, D. C. Johnston, R. Viswanathan, R. N. Shelton, L. E. DeLong, W. A. Fertig, J. Low Temp. Phys. 33, 175-203 (1978), DOI 10.1007/BF00117075. reader_a.paper_formula: WBe2
reader_a.at_pct_check: Paper formula WBe2: W = 1/3 = 33.33 at.%, Be = 2/3 = 66.67 at.%. Row: W 33.3, Be 66.7. Difference 0.03 at.% on each element (rounding only), inside the 0.15 at.% limit. Caveat on the real sample: the paper gives no chemical analysis. It says the lattice parameters are consistent with the W-rich side of the WBe2 homogeneity range, which the abstract gives as approximately W1.02Be1.98 to W0.88Be2.12. W-rich limit W1.02Be1.98: W = 1.02/3 = 34.00 at.%, Be = 66.00 at.%, i.e. 0.67 at.% from stoichiometric WBe2 (0.70 at.% from the row as rounded), which is outside 0.15 at.%. Be-rich limit W0.88Be2.12: W = 29.33 at.%, Be = 70.67 at.%. So the check passes on the formula the paper uses for its sample and compound (WBe2), but the paper does not pin the composition of the superconducting phase to within 0.15 at.%; it could lie anywhere from 33.3 to about 34.0 at.% W. Whole-button composition (phase plus free W) is more W-rich still: with 5-10% free W it is roughly 34.5 to 36 at.% W (my arithmetic, taking the paper's '~5-10%' as either mole or weight fraction; the paper does not say which).
reader_a.phase_or_sample: Bulk polycrystalline arc-melted button; resistivity on a slice about 0.5 mm thick, specific heat on the same piece. Hexagonal WBe2, space group 194 (P63/mmc), a = 4.452 A, c = 7.309 A. Not strictly single phase: X-ray pattern shows about 5-10% W metal; authors estimate less than 2% WBe13 or WBe22 and 'approximately 90-95% pure WBe2' (the abstract calls it 'essentially single phase WBe2'). Authors place the sample on the W-rich side of the homogeneity range.
reader_a.source_url: https://arxiv.org/pdf/2411.17504
reader_a.page_table_or_figure: arXiv:2411.17504v1 PDF (10 pages; page numbers are of this PDF, not the journal): abstract, p. 2 (bulk superconductor at ambient pressure, Tc onset 1.05 K, zero resistance ~0.86 K, homogeneity range); Section 2 and Fig. 1, pp. 3-4 (phase content, lattice parameters, W-rich side); Section 3.1 and Fig. 2, pp. 4-5 (zero-field resistivity, onset 1.05 K, zero below 0.86 K); Fig. 3, p. 6 (resistivity in field, Tc 1.05/0.91/0.67/0.51 K at 0/0.01/0.02/0.03 T); Section 3.2 and Fig. 4, pp. 6-7 (specific heat, onset 0.88 K, midpoint 0.72 K, deltaC/(gamma*Tc_mid) = 1.08); Conclusions, p. 7.
reader_a.tc_criterion: Resistive onset in zero field (start of the drop, marked in Fig. 2 at the crossing of two straight lines). Other values in the same paper: resistivity reaches zero below about 0.86 K; specific-heat onset about 0.88 K, specific-heat midpoint 0.72 K, peak at about 0.7 K.
reader_a.pressure: ambient (the abstract says 'a bulk superconductor at ambient pressure'; no pressure cell was used)
reader_a.measurement_method: Four-wire DC electrical resistivity, 0.3 to 5 K, in zero field and in 0.01, 0.02 and 0.03 T; specific heat by the time-constant method on the same piece; powder X-ray diffraction. No magnetisation or Meissner measurement is reported.
reader_a.synthesis_conditions: Arc-melting of W foil (99.95%) with Be pieces (99.999%); melting point of WBe2 given as about 2200 C. Section 2: about 30% excess Be, melted six times, about 5% Be lost per melt. Abstract: prepared with a slight (~5%) excess of W to avoid WBe13 and WBe22. No anneal is described.
reader_a.quote: The resistivity in zero and applied fields and specific heat data indicate that our sample of WBe2 is a bulk superconductor at ambient pressure with a Tconset in ρ at 1.05 K, and Tc(ρ→0) at ~0.86 K.
reader_a.evidence_note: I read the whole arXiv preprint (v1, 26 Nov 2024) and looked at Figs. 1-4; I did not open the publisher's version of record. The text states superconductivity for WBe2, in a bulk sample, at ambient pressure, with a Tc: abstract as quoted; Section 3.1 'these resistivity data indicate that WBe2 is a superconductor itself'; Section 3.2 says the resistive transition 'corresponds to a bulk superconducting transition in the whole sample as measured by the specific heat'; Conclusions 'we have discovered bulk superconductivity in WBe2 at 1 K'. Fig. 4 is annotated Tc(mid) = 0.72 K, deltaC/Tc(mid) = 3.83 mJ/mol K2, deltaC/(gamma*Tc(mid)) = 1.08, Tc(onset) = 0.88 K, C/T = 3.54 + 0.0527 T2. Points a sceptic should weigh. (1) Composition: the formula check passes, but the sample was not chemically analysed and the authors put it on the W-rich side of a homogeneity range whose W-rich end is 0.67 at.% from WBe2; see at_pct_check. (2) Phase purity: about 5-10% free W and under 2% WBe13/WBe22. The authors attribute the transition to WBe2, not to an impurity: there is no feature at 4.1 K, where WBe13 and WBe22 superconduct, and the specific-heat anomaly is described as bulk. My own inference, not the paper's wording: a 5-10% minority phase could not give a specific-heat jump of 1.08 gamma*Tc for the whole sample. (3) Which Tc: 1.05 K is the resistive onset; the bulk thermodynamic transition is lower (onset 0.88 K, midpoint 0.72 K). (4) The abstract ('~5% excess of W') and Section 2 ('~30%' excess Be against evaporation) describe the starting mix differently; the two can be reconciled but the paper does not do so explicitly. (5) Prior null: the paper cites Alekseevskii and Mikhailov, Sov. Phys. JETP 16, 1493 (1963), as finding no superconductivity in WBe2 down to 1.68 K; that is above the Tc reported here, so the two do not conflict. I did not read the 1963 paper. (6) This is the only report I found; no replication and no contrary measurement below 1.68 K turned up in my searches. The quote flattens subscripts and superscripts (WBe2, Tc with superscript onset).

refutation_attempts: Source re-read: downloaded arXiv:2411.17504v1 (10-page text PDF, only version listed; abstract page gives DOI 10.1016/j.jallcom.2024.177756), read all text with pdftotext and viewed pages 3-7 (Figs. 1-4) as images. The figures match the text: Fig. 2 shows rho falling from about 6.6 to about 0 microOhm-cm between about 1.05 and 0.86 K; Fig. 3 shows the drop moving to 0.91, 0.67 and 0.51 K in 0.01, 0.02 and 0.03 T, so it is field dependent like superconductivity; Fig. 4 shows a C/T jump from about 3.6 to about 7.3 mJ/mol K2, annotated Tc(onset) = 0.88 K, Tc(mid) = 0.72 K, deltaC/(gamma Tc(mid)) = 1.08.

Version of record: one Firecrawl scrape of the DOI landing page (ScienceDirect, PII S0925838824043445, J. Alloys Compd. 1010, 177756, 5 Jan 2025). Its abstract matches the arXiv abstract word for word on the deciding sentence, and its highlights read 'Superconductivity found at Tc = 1.05 K in WBe2' and 'Bulk specific heat anomaly at Tc'. No correction or erratum notice on the page; 'Cited by (1)' is an unrelated ZrSe2 monolayer calculation (also confirmed with FastTrack get_citations).

Composition arithmetic: WBe2 gives W = 1/3 = 0.33333 and Be = 2/3 = 0.66667. Row: W 0.333, Be 0.667. Differences 0.033 at.% on each element, inside 0.15 at.%. Caveat: there was no chemical analysis. The paper gives the WBe2 homogeneity range as about W1.02Be1.98 (W 34.00 at.%, 0.70 at.% from the row) to W0.88Be2.12 (W 29.33 at.%), and places its sample on the W-rich side from the lattice parameters (a = 4.452 A, c = 7.309 A). The midpoint of that range is W0.95Be2.05 (W 31.67 at.%), so 'W-rich side' covers about 31.7 to 34.0 at.% W, which includes stoichiometric WBe2 (33.33 at.%). The rule compares the paper's formula with the row, and that passes. The true phase composition is not pinned to within 0.15 at.%; I record this but do not count it as a refutation, because the table's zero label also refers to the compound by its formula WBe2.
Bulk or film: bulk. Arc-melted polycrystalline button; resistivity on a ~0.5 mm thick slice; specific heat on the same piece. No film or nanostructure.
Pressure: ambient. The abstract says 'a bulk superconductor at ambient pressure'. The high-pressure work is only motivation (MoB2, WB2) and planned future work.

Phase purity and impurity attribution. XRD (Fig. 1) shows about 5-10% W metal, indexed as bcc Im-3m alpha-W (the blue reference pattern in Fig. 1), and under 2% WBe13 or WBe22 (no peaks near 13 or 22 deg 2theta). Could the ~1 K transition come from a minority phase? (a) alpha-W: bulk Tc is about 0.01 K. The FastTrack abstract of Basavaiah and Pollack (J. Appl. Phys. 1968, doi 10.1063/1.1656012) gives the bulk value as 0.01 K and puts the 3.2 K tungsten value in beta-W (A15) films; the paper's XRD shows bcc W, not A15. (b) WBe13/WBe22 superconduct at 4.1 K, and Fig. 2 shows no feature there. (c) Be: bulk Tc is far below 0.3 K (my background knowledge, not from a source opened here; it is not needed for the verdict). (d) The decisive point is the specific heat: a jump of deltaC/(gamma Tc) = 1.08 measured on the whole piece. The authors state it is 'a bulk superconducting transition in the whole sample'. A 5-10% minority phase could not give a jump of that size unless its electronic specific heat were many times that of WBe2; this is my inference. The superconductivity belongs to the WBe2 phase.

Which Tc: the resistive onset is 1.05 K (the paper's headline and its highlights), rho reaches 0 below ~0.86 K, the specific-heat onset is 0.88 K and the midpoint is 0.72 K. The authors attribute the spread to the homogeneity range. All of these are well below 1.68 K, the lowest temperature of the earlier null.

sceptic.evidence_note: The version of record and the arXiv v1 state the same thing. Abstract: 'our sample of WBe2 is a bulk superconductor at ambient pressure with a Tconset in ρ at 1.05 K, and Tc(ρ→0) at ∼0.86 K.' Sec. 3.2: the resistive transition 'corresponds to a bulk superconducting transition in the whole sample as measured by the specific heat'. Conclusions: 'we have discovered bulk superconductivity in WBe2 at 1 K.' This is a single report from one group and one sample, not replicated. The earlier null (1963) only reached 1.68 K, which explains the table's zero without contradicting the new result. The phase composition is not chemically analysed (W-rich side of a homogeneity range whose W-rich limit is 0.70 at.% from the row), and the paper's formula is stoichiometric WBe2.
sceptic.verifier_reason: I tried to refute both readers and could not. I re-read the full arXiv text and figures myself and checked the publisher's abstract and highlights for the version of record. The paper states bulk superconductivity in WBe2 at ambient pressure with a Tc: resistive onset 1.05 K, zero resistance below 0.86 K, and a specific-heat anomaly (onset 0.88 K, midpoint 0.72 K, deltaC/(gamma Tc) = 1.08) that the authors attribute to the whole sample. The formula WBe2 matches the row Be:0.667;W:0.333 to 0.033 at.%. The sample is an arc-melted bulk button measured at ambient pressure. The only minority phases are alpha-W (bulk Tc about 0.01 K) and under 2% WBe13/WBe22, whose 4.1 K transition is absent. The size of the specific-heat jump rules out a minority phase as the source, so the superconductivity belongs to WBe2. The only contrary report found (Alekseevskii and Mikhailov 1963, cited by the paper) measured only down to 1.68 K, so it does not conflict and is the probable source of the table's zero. The strongest candidate for a sub-1 K null, Rapp et al. 1974, did not test WBe2. Remaining weaknesses, which a human auditor should weigh but which I do not judge to be refutations under the owner's rule: one unreplicated report; no chemical analysis, with the WBe2 phase possibly up to ~0.7 at.% W-rich of stoichiometry; and a Tc that depends on the criterion (1.05 K resistive onset versus 0.72 K thermodynamic midpoint). The STATED route is met, so the label should be corrected.

reader_a.evidence_note: Three primary leads were identified but none could be opened from here. (1) Ralls, Rose, Wulff, J. Appl. Phys. 51, 3316 (1980), DOI 10.1063/1.328039 (confirmed by OpenAlex): its abstract says resistive Jc, critical fields and normal-state resistivities were obtained at 4.2 K for 55 Nb-Ti-Zr alloys. It gives no compositions and no Tc. Even if the full text lists this alloy with a critical field at 4.2 K, that would only show Tc > 4.2 K, not a Tc as route STATED requires. (2) Zwicker, Meier, Roeschel, J. Less-Common Met. 14, 253 (1968), DOI 10.1016/0022-5088(68)90031-3 (confirmed by OpenAlex). The German abstract, read via SciSpace, gives a 900 C section with a miscibility gap reaching 51 at.% Ti and 19 at.% Zr. It reports transition-temperature changes for alloys with 36 at.% and about 20 at.% Nb, and Jc of Ti-Nb wires near valence-electron concentration 4.2 raised by 7 at.% Zr. It gives no Tc for this composition. (3) Lazarev et al. 1970, DOI 10.1007/978-1-4684-8220-1_15: its abstract reports Tc of cast and annealed Nb-Zr-Ti alloys, where a rise in Tc on annealing is due to precipitation of a Nb-rich phase (multiphase samples). It gives no compositions. The open-access Horiuchi, Monju, Nagai paper (J. Japan Inst. Metals 37, 882, 1973; DOI 10.2320/jinstmet1952.37.8_882) was read in full: Table 2 lists 31 nominal compositions, all containing 5 or 10 at.% Ta, so none is the ternary row. Kadykova and Surovaya 1967 (DOI 10.1007/BF00654306; abstract only) studied Nb-Ti-Zr alloys with 47-53 at.% Nb, which matches this row's Nb, but the abstract gives no Ti/Zr split and no Tc. All bcc Nb-Ti-Zr alloys in this region are expected to superconduct near 9 K, but no source I opened states a Tc for this composition, so the label cannot be corrected under the owner's rule.

Technol. 19 (2006) 623-628) and read the whole text with pdftotext; checked Table 1 and Fig. 7 on the rendered page image (PDF p. 14). Table 1 is as both readers give it: nominal B/Nb 2.0 / Rietveld 2.00(1) / XPS 2.00 / Tc 0; 2.1 / 2.10(1) / 2.14 / 0; 2.2 / 2.20(2) / 2.15 / 5.20 K; 2.3 / 2.30(1) / 2.27 / 9.40 K; 2.4 / 2.32(1) / 2.31 / 9.65 K; 2.5 / 2.34(1) / 2.44 / 9.75 K (Tc column '+-0.05').

Arithmetic: row B/Nb = 0.691/0.309 = 2.236 (Nb1-xB2 with x = 0.106). Nominal/Rietveld 2.2 -> 68.750 at.% B (0.35 below); 2.3 -> 69.697 (0.60 above). XPS 2.15 -> 68.254 (0.85 below); 2.27 -> 69.419 (0.32 above). The bracket holds within 2 at.% on every scale; the readers' arithmetic is correct. But the XPS compositions carry +-3% (the column header says so): 2.15 +-3% spans 67.59-68.89 at.% B and 2.27 +-3% spans 68.77-70.04 at.% B, which contains the row; the non-superconducting XPS 2.14 sample (68.15 at.%) and the superconducting XPS 2.15 sample (68.25 at.%) are 0.10 at.% apart, inside that error. The onset of superconductivity is therefore not resolved, and the row sits at that onset.

Bulk / phase purity: the SuST paper is an XPS study; it does not report superconducting volume fraction, does not define the Tc criterion, and takes the Tc values from the group's earlier paper (J. Phys.: Condens. Matter 16 (2004) 5979, closed access; abstract read via OpenAlex: magnetization 2-15 K, superconductivity for (B/Nb)exp >= 2.20(2)). It states NbB2 is 'larger than 94%' of every sample, so the series is not shown to be single-phase and the up-to-6% other phase is not named. Nothing in the text read shows that the 5.2 K signal of the lower bracket sample (nominal 2.2) is bulk.

Same-route independent check: Mudgel et al. (arXiv 0807.1198, Solid State Commun. 2008, DOI 10.1016/j.ssc.2008.07.006), read in full: commercial NbB2 + B, sealed (iron) tube, 1100 C, Ar, quenched, i.e. essentially the Escamilla route at ambient pressure. Their NbB2.2 (Rietveld B/Nb 2.184, 68.59 at.% B, 0.51 at.% below the row) 'gives a very weak diamagnetic signal at a temperature of about 8.9K, which can only be seen in the enlarged view'. In Fig. 4 (rendered PDF p. 12) its ZFC moment at 5 K is about -0.0016 emu/g against about -0.19 emu/g for NbB2.4, i.e. under 1% of the bulk signal: trace, not bulk, superconductivity at the lower bracket composition. Bulk superconductivity ('sufficient superconducting volume fraction') appears only at NbB2.4 (Rietveld 2.405, 70.63 at.% B, 1.53 at.% above the row).

Second independent check: Xiao et al. (arXiv cond-mat/0603706, Phys. Rev. B 73, 224516 (2006)), read in full: nominal Nb1-xB2, 6 GPa synthesis from Nb + amorphous B, measured by DC susceptibility. For 0 <= x < 0.2 (which includes nominal Nb0.9B2 = 68.97 at.% B, 0.13 at.% from the row) only 'very weak diamagnetism' is seen, which the authors attribute to 'a superconducting impurity, such as unreacted Nb-metal'; they conclude superconductivity 'chiefly exists in the range of 0.2<x<0.4'. High-pressure synthesis and nominal composition, so not a clean null, but a third group placing the row's composition below the bulk-superconducting range.

Third series: Yamamoto et al. (arXiv cond-mat/0208331, Physica C 383 (2002) 197), read: large volume fraction and Tc above 8.5 K for 0.08 <= x < 0.24 (nominal Nb0.92B2, 68.49 at.% B, Tc 9.0 K; Nb0.84B2, 70.42 at.% B, Tc 9.1 K), but all made at 5 GPa; the authors state the 9 K superconductivity 'is clearly owed to the pressure' and report Tc 5.3 K for Nb0.84B2 made at ambient pressure. EPMA gave Nb0.76B2.0 for nominal Nb0.84B2, so nominal compositions in this system can be off by several at.%. Not usable as an ambient-pressure bracket.

Process dependence: Takeya et al., Physica C (2004), DOI 10.1016/j.physc.2004.02.046 (abstract via SciSpace): the ~9 K superconducting NbB2 phase was 'induced by a rapid-quenching process and disappeared by annealing at 1100 C' for NbxB2, x = 0.67-1.11. Whether a given Nb-deficient NbB2 sample superconducts depends on heat treatment, which makes the row's two SuperCon zero reports plausible as real measurements.

sceptic.verifier_reason: The readers read Table 1 correctly and the at.% arithmetic holds: the row (B/Nb 2.236, 69.10 at.% B) lies between Escamilla & Huerta's nominal 2.2 (Tc 5.20 K) and 2.3 (Tc 9.40 K) samples, each within 2 at.%. The doubt is about substance. (1) The BRACKETED route asks for a single-phase series. This one is only described as more than 94% NbB2, the other phase is not named, and the paper read (an XPS study) gives no superconducting volume fraction and no Tc criterion for the Tc values it quotes from the group's closed-access 2004 paper. So nothing read shows that the 5.2 K signal of the lower bracket sample is bulk. (2) Two independent groups found only trace superconductivity at this boron content. Mudgel et al. used essentially the same ambient-pressure route and got a very weak signal for NbB2.2 (Rietveld 2.184, 0.51 at.% from the row), under 1% of the bulk NbB2.4 signal. Their next sample is bulk only at 70.6 at.% B. Xiao et al. found only weak diamagnetism, which they assign to an impurity such as unreacted Nb, for nominal Nb0.9B2, 0.13 at.% from the row. (3) Escamilla's own XPS compositions (+-3%) do not resolve the onset: a non-superconducting sample at 68.15 at.% B and a superconducting one at 68.25 at.% B. The row is closer to the lower, doubtful sample than to the 9.4 K one. (4) Takeya et al. report that the superconducting phase in Nb-deficient NbB2 depends on processing and disappears on annealing at 1100 C, so the table's two zero reports at exactly this composition may be real measurements; I could not identify their source. Taken together, the row sits at the edge of the bulk-superconducting range, where results depend on the sample. I cannot say without doubt that a bulk sample of this composition superconducts at ambient pressure. Under the owner's rule, when in doubt, the label stays. Lead for library access: Escamilla et al., J. Phys.: Condens. Matter 16 (2004) 5979, DOI 10.1088/0953-8984/16/32/029. Check its M(T) curves and shielding fraction for the B/Nb 2.2 sample and the identity of the minority phase. If the 2.2 sample shows a substantial bulk shielding fraction from a single NbB2 phase, the bracket would stand and this row could be reconsidered.

Arithmetic on the paper's written formula: Ir3Te8 gives Ir = 3/11 = 0.272727, Te = 8/11 = 0.727273. Row: Ir 0.272, Te 0.728. Differences 0.000727 each, i.e. 0.073 at.%, inside 0.15 at.%. The row corresponds to x = 2 x 0.272/0.728 = 0.747 in IrxTe2, or IrTe2.676.

Arithmetic on the paper's own structure refinement: Sec. IV of both versions says 'The Ir site occupancy was freely varied and found to be 80%'. Exact Ir3Te8 is 75% occupancy of the four pyrite Ir sites. Read as 80% of the Ir sites of Ir4Te8 (the authors refine one cubic-like cell, a = 6.4024 A, alpha = 90.017 deg), the crystal is Ir3.2Te8 = Ir0.80Te2: Ir = 0.8/2.8 = 0.285714, Te = 0.714286, which is 1.37 at.% from the row on each element, about nine times the 0.15 at.% limit. The published version adds that this 80% occupation causes disorder scattering and the large residual resistivity, so the authors treat it as a real property of the measured crystal, not a fitting artefact. EDX was done but no EDX composition appears in the text of either version. The paper never states that the measured crystals are Ir3Te8 within any stated tolerance; Ir3Te8 is the nominal (starting) stoichiometry of the synthesis.

Composition sensitivity in this system: Qi et al., PRL 109, 217002 (arXiv:1210.5353, read in full) describe Ir0.75Ch2 (Ir3Ch8) as 'close to the boundary between metallic and insulating states', with superconductivity appearing and Tc rising as x increases (Te maximum 4.7 K at x = 0.93; Te series only in the Supplementary Material, which I could not open). Li, Yan, Singh, Goodenough and Zhou, PRB 92, 155118 (arXiv:1505.06124, read): 'The C-Ir1-xTe2 is a superconductor with Tc =1.8 - 4.7 K depending on the Ir nonstoichiometry x' and 'Tc increases monotonically with decreasing x' (x = Ir deficiency). So a shift of 1.4 at.% Ir is not negligible here: the row sits at the Ir-poor end where superconductivity weakens or vanishes, and the measured crystal, by its own refinement, lies on the Ir-rich side.

Bulk and phase check: millimetre single crystals, flux-grown from excess Te, no pressure cell anywhere in the text (ambient by implication). Single-crystal XRD: R-3 below TS = 350 K, Pa-3 above; R = 0.025, Rw = 0.058; superlattice from ordered Ir vacancies; no second phase reported. But the transition is incomplete: in the published version the a-axis resistivity drops by one order of magnitude from 1.80 K to 1.2 K and does not vanish (4.5e-5 ohm cm at 1.2 K); in arXiv v2 Fig. 3a (data to 1.7 K) the zero-field drop seen is from about 0.458 to below 0.445 mohm cm; ZFC and FC susceptibility hardly differ down to 0.5 K and the Meissner fraction is about 16% at 0.5 K (my own check: a full-shielding value for Ir3Te8 with a 262 A^3 cell is about -12.6 emu/mol, and Fig. 3b reaches about -2 emu/mol at 0.5 K, about 16%). I could not see Fig. 4 (heat capacity), which is on the unfetched pages. In the same compound family, Li et al. PRB 92, 155118 read a resistive drop that does not reach zero at 1.8 K as 'filamentary superconductivity' and attributed it to an Ir-richer cubic Ir1-xTe2 impurity in their own sample; a similar origin (Ir-rich regions, given the 80% occupancy and the authors' own remark on 'possible existence of inhomogeneities') cannot be excluded from what I read, although the heat-capacity jump argues against a small impurity fraction.

Pressure: none applied; the paper's measurements are in QD PPMS/MPMS and a closed-cycle cryostat. Qi et al.'s IrxTe2 samples are synthesized at 5 GPa but measured at ambient pressure; they are a different polymorph (cubic high-pressure phase) from the ambient-pressure rhombohedral crystals of Li et al.

B 87, 174510; DOI verified) name their single crystals Ir3Te8, that Ir3Te8 matches the row within 0.073 at.%, that the samples are bulk and measured without applied pressure, and that the authors call the 1.8 K transition bulk superconductivity of Ir3Te8. But the paper's own text gives a reason of substance to doubt that the measured crystal has the row's composition: its single-crystal refinement finds an Ir site occupancy of 80%, not the 75% of Ir3Te8, i.e. about Ir0.80Te2 (Ir 28.6 at.%), 1.37 at.% from the row, nine times the 0.15 at.% limit; the authors treat this occupancy as real (they blame it for the large residual resistivity) and give no EDX composition. In this system superconductivity depends strongly on Ir content: Qi et al. place Ir0.75Te2 at the metal-insulator boundary with superconductivity emerging as Ir increases, and Li et al. (PRB 92, 155118) report Tc rising monotonically with Ir content; the row (x = 0.747) sits at the Ir-poor edge and the measured crystal on the Ir-rich side of it. The transition is also incomplete (no zero resistance down to 1.2 K, Meissner fraction about 16% at 0.5 K, ZFC close to FC), the bulk claim rests on a heat-capacity jump whose figure I could not see, and the result has not been reproduced by any other group I could find. reader_a.quote: Since over the wide composition range the critical temperature was found to be over 8°K, there is the possibility that these alloys can be used as solenoids for the superconducting magnet.
reader_a.evidence_note: I read the full text of the lead paper, Doi, Mitani and Umezawa, J. Japan Inst. Metals 30(2), 133-138 (1966), through a text extraction of the open-access J-STAGE PDF (6 of 6 pages; Japanese with English abstract, tables and captions). It measured Tc on 33 analysed Nb-Zr-Ti samples. No sample has the row's composition: the nearest, No. 825 (Nb 80.0 / Zr 10.0 / Ti 10.0), is 3.0 at.% away in Nb and in Zr, and the next along the same Ti = 10 at.% section, No. 725, is 7.0 at.% away. So this paper neither states superconductivity for Nb 77 / Ti 10 / Zr 13 nor brackets it within 2 at.%. The quote is the paper's general statement in its English abstract (text as in the FastTrack/OpenAlex record of the abstract; the same sentence is in the PDF text); it is not a statement about this composition. The extraction is machine-read text of a scanned 1966 paper and shows some reading errors in figure data, but the Table 3 rows quoted here each sum to 100 at.% and agree with the figure legends. The other leads, Ralls, Rose and Wulff 1980, Zwicker, Meier and Roeschel 1968, and Lazarev et al. 1970, are paywalled; I saw only their abstracts, none of which names this composition or gives a Tc for it. The abstract of Ralls et al. reports critical current densities, resistive critical fields and resistivities at 4.2 K for 55 alloys and mentions no Tc measurements.
reader_a.reason_if_not: No primary paper that I could open reports a measurement on Nb 77 / Ti 10 / Zr 13 at.% within 0.15 at.%, or a single-phase series with measured superconducting samples within 2 at.% on both sides. The one paper read in full (Doi et al. 1966) has its nearest samples 3.0 and 7.0 at.% away. The papers most likely to contain this exact composition (Ralls et al. 1980; Zwicker et al. 1968; Lazarev et al. 1970) are paywalled and were not read. The source of the row's composition was not identified.
leads_for_library: Ralls, Rose, Wulff, J. Appl. Phys. 51(6), 3316-3321 (1980), DOI 10.1063/1.328039: 55 Nb-Ti-Zr alloys measured at 4.2 K. reader_a.quote: Since over the wide composition range the critical temperature was found to be over 8°K, there is the possibility that these alloys can be used as solenoids for the superconducting magnet.
reader_a.evidence_note: I read the full text of the paper through a text extraction of the open-access PDF. What the text shows: (1) Table 3 lists sample No. 825 with analysed composition Nb 80.0, Zr 10.0, Ti 10.0 at%, an exact match to the row. (2) The method section says Tc was measured inductively on the cast ingots, that the wires for the other measurements were made from the samples whose Tc measurement was finished, and that critical current was measured on all samples. (3) Fig. 3 plots Tc for the Nb-Zr-Ti alloys on the composition triangle. The extraction returned the numbers printed in Fig. 3 but not the alloy point each belongs to: 10.01, 9.15, 10.25, 10.93, 10.14, 10.07, 9.74, 9.93, 9.60, 9.16, 9.09, 9.48, 9.44, 9.85, 9.91, 9.82, 9.17, 8.85, 8.53, 8.5, 8.22, 8.49, 8.00, 7.99, 7.39, 6.01, 7.13 (K), and possibly also 10.79, 10.45, 10.32, 9.70, 9.33, which appeared in a second column without a decimal point. Every number is between 6.01 and 10.93 K; none is zero. (4) The Discussion (p. 137) says, in my translation, that the Tc of the Nb-Zr-Ti alloys under study are all near 10 K (Japanese text with the formula markup removed: 'Nb-Zr-Ti系合金の Tc はすべて 10°K 近辺であり'). (5) The English abstract says Tc was over 8 K over the wide composition range. So the paper lists this exact composition as a measured bulk sample and reports only superconducting alloys, but I could not read which Tc number belongs to this sample. US patent 3,408,604 by the same group (opened on Google Patents) has the same Tc triangle as its FIGURE 2 and says alloys with a small amount of Ti and about 10 to 35% Zr have Tc above 10.5 K; its text gives no Tc for 80/10/10 either. The patent is not a paper and was used only as a lead.
reader_a.reason_if_not: The STATED route needs the paper to state a Tc for this composition, and I did not read one. The Tc of sample No. 825 is a number printed at the point Nb 80 / Zr 10 / Ti 10 at% in Fig. 3 (p. 135). I could reach the paper only as extracted text, in which the Fig. 3 numbers are not attached to compositions, so I cannot say which number is this sample's, or prove from the figure that this sample has a labelled point. Everything else checks: exact composition match in Table 3, bulk ingot, inductive Tc method, no pressure, and no non-superconducting alloy reported. The only missing item is the Tc value at this point of Fig. 3. I did not treat the general remark 'all near 10 K' as a Tc for this sample, because the same paper has alloys at 6.01 to 8.5 K under that remark.
