reader_a.measurement_method: dc SQUID magnetization (ZFC at 0.5 mT, Fig. 5; measured from 2 K); four-point resistivity (Fig. 3); zero-field and longitudinal-field muon-spin spectroscopy for the magnetic order; 19F NMR for the fluorine content.
reader_a.synthesis_conditions: Solid-state reaction of stoichiometric CeAs, Fe2O3, FeF2 and Fe. CeAs was made from Ce chips and As pieces at 450-500 C for 4 days. The mixed powders were pressed into pellets and heated to about 1100 C for 50 h.
reader_a.quote: Samples with x ≳ 0.06 display a clear transition to the superconducting state, as shown by the low-temperature ZFC magnetization data for x = 0.06 and 0.07 reported in Fig. 5.
reader_a.evidence_note: Source read in full: arXiv:1109.3170v1, the only arXiv version, whose arXiv page gives the related DOI 10.1103/PhysRevB.84.195123. The journal version itself was not opened (paywalled); the journal abstract, which I did see, says superconductivity appears for x > 0.04. Table I of the preprint lists five samples: x(F) = 0, 0.03(1), 0.04(1) with no Tc, then x(F) = 0.06(1) with Tc = 26.5(5) K and T_N = 28.0(7) K, and x(F) = 0.07(1) with Tc = 18.3(5) K and T_N = 16.5(3) K. Fig. 5 shows the zero-field-cooled SQUID susceptibility at 0.5 mT for x = 0.06 and 0.07: the x = 0.06 curve turns diamagnetic at the arrow Tc2 (about 26.5 K by my reading) and reaches about -0.45 in SI units near 10 K (my reading of the plot). Fig. 3 shows the normalized resistivity of the x = 0.06(1) sample falling to zero at low temperature (my reading of the plot; the text does not comment on it). The text says the muon data show that 'all these samples show bulk superconductivity'. The same sample has short-range magnetic order in 100(3)% of its volume below 28 K, so the authors describe coexistence of the two orders on a nanometre scale. x is not the nominal content: it is the 'real' fluorine content from the 19F NMR signal intensity, corrected for CeOF found by Rietveld refinement, and the paper says the real content is systematically lower than the nominal one. Supporting primary source, also read: Maeter et al., arXiv:1210.6959v1 (a preprint with no journal reference on its arXiv page; a different group and different samples, F content by nuclear quadrupole resonance). It reports CeFeAsO1-xFx with x = 0.063(2) as a bulk superconductor, Tc = 29.5 K from resistivity and 29.8(2) K from muon data (p. 17 and Table III, p. 29); x = 0.063 gives F = 0.063/4 = 1.575 at.% and O = 0.937/4 = 23.425 at.%, each 0.075 at.% from the row, so it is also inside the limit. The same preprint says its x = 0.048(3) sample is not a bulk superconductor (resistivity drops 'only almost to zero', attributed to spurious superconducting grains). Related source, read: Sanna et al., arXiv:1007.5460v1 (Phys. Rev. B 82, 060508(R), DOI 10.1103/PhysRevB.82.060508) reports one polycrystalline sample with x = 0.06(2), Tc = 18 K by SQUID and a roughly 50% superconducting volume fraction; the Shiroka preprint later cites that study as the x = 0.07 case, and its own x = 0.07(1) sample has Tc = 18.3(5) K, so I do not count the Sanna sample as evidence for x = 0.06 (x = 0.07 is F = 1.75 at.%, 0.25 at.% from the row). CONTRARY REPORT, read: Zhao et al., arXiv:0806.2528 (Nature Materials 7, 953, DOI 10.1038/nmat2315), p. 4 of the preprint: 'polycrystalline nonsuperconducting CeFeAsO1-xFx with x = 0, 0.02, 0.04, 0.06 (as confirmed by measurements using a commercial SQUID)'. That passage gives no lowest temperature for the SQUID check and does not say how x was determined, so it does not meet the verified_null definition, but it is a primary report that a sample labelled x = 0.06 did not superconduct. The two reports use different composition scales (measured F content in Shiroka; an unspecified, probably starting, composition in Zhao), and this composition sits at the edge of the superconducting range, where a change of 0.01 in x changes the answer. Chen et al., arXiv:0803.3790 (Phys. Rev. Lett. 100, 247002) was read and has no x = 0.06 sample (its samples are x = 0, 0.04, 0.08, 0.12, 0.16, 0.20). My verdict is 'confirmed' because the STATED route is met by the Shiroka table as written; the sceptic should weigh the Zhao report and the +/- 0.01 uncertainty on x.

refutation_attempts: Source re-read. Shiroka et al. Table I (preprint p. 5) does list x(F) = 0.06(1) with Tc = 26.5(5) K, TN = 28.0(7) K and magnetic fraction 100(3)%; Sec. II.D item iv (p. 4) says samples with x of about 0.06 and above show a clear superconducting transition in ZFC magnetization (Fig. 5), and that TF-muSR shows bulk superconductivity, with the detailed TF data given only for the x = 0.07 sample in their Ref. 21. The readers transcribed this correctly.

Arithmetic. CeFeAsO0.94F0.06 has 4 atoms per formula unit: Ce = Fe = As = 1/4 = 0.2500; O = 0.94/4 = 0.2350; F = 0.06/4 = 0.0150. Row: As 0.250, Ce 0.250, F 0.015, Fe 0.250, O 0.235. Difference 0.00 at.% on every element for the stated central value. But the paper's own uncertainty, x = 0.06(1), is F = 1.50 +/- 0.25 at.% and O = 23.50 -/+ 0.25 at.%, wider than the 0.15 at.% limit; the Fig. 2 caption gives Delta-x/x of about 25%.

Composition scale. Shiroka et al. label samples by the 19F NMR fluorine content and state that 'the real F content is systematically lower than the nominal one'; no nominal value is given for this sample, and Appendix A calls the SEM sample 'a nominal x = 0.06', which is inconsistent with that labelling. Table I gives Tc = 26.5 K for x = 0.06 but 18.3 K for x = 0.07, the reverse of the usual rise of Tc with F at the edge of the dome, so the 0.01 step between these two labels is not resolved by the data. The same group's earlier sample with 'a best estimate of x = 0.06(2)' and Tc = 18 K (Sanna et al. 2010) is referred to in the 2011 paper as the x = 0.07 case.

Bulk and pressure. Polycrystalline pressed pellets from solid-state reaction, SQUID and four-point resistivity, no pressure cell mentioned: bulk at ambient pressure by implication. Impurity: CeOF never above 2% vol; not a superconducting impurity. This part of the readers' case holds.

Phase. The superconductivity is attributed to the 1111 phase and coexists with short-range Fe magnetic order in 100% of the muon volume; the authors call this nanoscopic coexistence. The ZFC signal at 0.5 mT (about -0.45 SI near 10 K by my reading of Fig. 5) is partial; the bulk claim rests on TF-muSR shown in detail only for x = 0.07.

Contrary reports searched (FastTrack search for 'CeFeAsO0.94F0.06' and for underdoped CeFeAsO1-xFx x = 0.06; arXiv listing searches for 'CeFeAsO F 0.06', 'CeFeAsO1-xFx', 'CeFeAsO fluorine', 'CeOFeAs F'). Two primary reports found that measured a sample written CeFeAsO0.94F0.06 and found no superconductivity: Zhao et al. 2008 (SQUID, no temperature given) and Shang et al. 2013 (resistance with no drop, measured to about 0.5 K by my reading of the Fig. 2a inset). Both samples come from the Institute of Physics, Beijing (Chen/Wang group, the method of Chen et al. PRL 100, 247002, which states compositions from starting materials, i.e. nominal). sceptic.verifier_reason: The readers read Shiroka et al. correctly, and the arithmetic of the stated central value is exact: CeFeAsO0.94F0.06 is Ce = Fe = As = 25.00, O = 23.50, F = 1.50 at.%, the row exactly. The sample is a bulk polycrystal measured at ambient pressure, and the superconductivity belongs to the 1111 phase. But there is a reason of substance to doubt that this composition, as written, superconducts. Two primary papers measured a sample written CeFeAsO0.94F0.06 and found no superconductivity. Zhao et al., Nature Mater. 7, 953 (2008), checked theirs with a SQUID. Shang et al., J. Korean Phys. Soc. 62, 2001 (2013), measured resistance with no drop down to about 0.5 K and saw SDW order near 30 K. Both used nominal compositions from the Beijing synthesis route, and these are the likely source of the table's zeros. Shiroka et al. label their sample by an NMR-measured F content that they say is systematically below nominal. Its own uncertainty, x = 0.06(1), is +/- 0.25 at.% F, wider than the 0.15 at.% limit. Its Tc ordering (26.5 K at 0.06, 18.3 K at 0.07) shows the 0.01 steps between labels are not resolved, and the same group's earlier 'x = 0.06(2)' sample was later called x = 0.07. Maeter et al. place the onset of bulk superconductivity between measured x = 0.048 and 0.063. This row therefore sits exactly on the edge of the superconducting dome, where samples labelled x = 0.06 go either way depending on the composition scale and the batch. The 'not a superconductor' label has real primary support and is not shown to be wrong, so the correction should not be applied.

refutation_attempts: Source re-read: downloaded https://arxiv.org/pdf/2202.11355 myself (HTTP 200, 17 pages, single version v1 of 23 Feb 2022; the arXiv abstract page links DOI 10.1103/PhysRevB.105.214517). Read the methods sentence (PDF p. 4), the BaGa2 paragraph of Results (PDF pp. 7-8), the Fig. 3 caption (p. 10) and Table I (p. 14) with pdftotext, and viewed Fig. 3 (p. 13) as an image. The deciding statements are as both readers report: 'We found that the BaGa2 is indeed a superconductor with a measured Tc = 0.36 K'; onset about 0.37 K, 'Zero resistance is found below 0.29 K', AC susceptibility diamagnetic ('Meissner effect') below 0.32 K, 'A superconducting jump is found at 0.34 K and disappears under 5 kOe', BCS fit with Tc = 0.355 K. The published abstract (OpenAlex record of the PRB article) states the same: BaGa2 'is experimentally synthesized and measured to confirm that the compound is a Bardeen-Cooper-Schrieffer superconductor with Tc = 0.36 K'.
Composition arithmetic: BaGa2 = Ba 1/3 = 0.33333, Ga 2/3 = 0.66667. Row Ba 0.333, Ga 0.667. Differences 0.00033 on each element = 0.033 at.%, inside the 0.15 at.% limit. Holds.

Bulk or film: the paper says 'Single crystals of BaGa2 were grown by the self-flux method as reported previously[25]'. Bulk crystals, not a film or nanostructure. The specific-heat jump is a thermodynamic bulk probe; in Fig. 3c (my reading of the plot, not the paper's numbers) the 0 Oe data rise to about 4.6 mJ/mol K at about 0.34 K against about 2.4 mJ/mol K for the 5 kOe curve, with a normal-state C/T of roughly 7.5 mJ/mol K^2, i.e. a jump of the order of 0.8 gamma*Tc, and the 0 Oe data fall toward zero near 0.05 K with no large residual linear term. That size is not what a minor inclusion would give.

Pressure: measurements on a Quantum Design PPMS with a dilution refrigerator insert; no pressure cell or applied pressure is mentioned for BaGa2. Every mention of pressure in the text concerns other compounds (H3S, CaSi2, CaB2 synthesis routes). Ambient by implication; the words 'ambient pressure' are not used for this measurement.

Impurity phase: the crystals come from a self-flux growth, so I checked whether the transition could belong to a flux or side phase. Ref. 25 (Xu et al., arXiv:1907.10702, opened) gives the recipe: starting ratio Ba:Ga = 41.7:58.3 (Ba-rich relative to BaGa2), held at 950 C, cooled at 3 C/h to 700 C, flux centrifuged; composition checked by EDS and structure by XRD with refinement. Free alpha-Ga would superconduct near 1.08 K (Campanini et al. PRB 97, 184517 abstract gives alpha-Ga Tc < 1.2 K; beta-Ga 6.04 K); Fig. 3a shows flat normal-state resistance from 0.4 to 1.0 K and no feature near 1.08 K, so the 0.36 K transition is not Ga. Ba is not superconducting at ambient pressure. An arXiv search for BaGa4 and Ba8Ga7 returned no superconductivity report. No known Ba-Ga side phase accounts for 0.36 K, and the bulk-sized specific-heat jump points to the majority phase.

Weak points checked and not found decisive: (a) the paper itself shows no XRD or EDS of the measured crystals and relies on ref. 25; (b) Fig. 3b has a narrow positive spike in chi' (to about +5e-4 emu/Oe) just above the diamagnetic drop, which the text does not discuss; (c) 2*Delta0/kB*Tc = 2.83 is below the BCS 3.53; (d) only one group has reported the transition and no independent replication was found. None of these contradicts superconductivity of BaGa2: three independent probes (R to zero, diamagnetic chi', field-suppressed specific-heat jump) agree within 0.29-0.37 K on the same crystals.

Contrary-report search: arXiv full-text search 'BaGa2' and 'BaGa$_2$' (found 2202.11355, 2201.00172 theory, 1907.10702, 2510.05304); arXiv searches for the 2002 Physica C AlB2 survey, for Imai's M(Ga,Si)2 series and for SrGa2 superconductivity; FastTrack search_papers 'BaGa2 superconductivity low temperature measurement' and 'AlB2-type alkaline earth digallide SrGa2 BaGa2 superconducting transition experiment'; FastTrack get_citations on the PRB DOI (25 most-cited citing papers; none reports a failed replication). Wiley Scholar Gateway was tried for the 2009 Chem. Eur. J. full text but its free quota is exhausted (no search performed). OpenAlex key had 5 credits left after one get_work and was not used further.

Where the table's zeros likely come from: the row's sources are 'hosono;supercon'. Hosono et al., STAM 16, 033503 (2015) (arXiv:1505.02240, opened), Table 2(b) 'Materials which exhibited no superconductivity', lists BaGa2 in a shaded cell (legend: shaded = 'possible to obtain the target phase'; PDF p. 135, section 'Square net of traditional elements'); the table states no lowest temperature. The SuperCon zeros plausibly come from screens such as Meng et al., Physica C 382, 113 (2002) (paywalled, no abstract, not read) or Haarmann et al. (2009), whose abstract reports no phase transition between 1.8 and 320 K. All nulls found stop at or are not stated below about 1.8 K, above the reported Tc of 0.36 K, so they do not contradict it.

sceptic.verifier_reason: I re-read the arXiv full text of Phys. Rev. B 105, 214517 (2022) and its Fig. 3 myself and could not refute the readers. The composition is BaGa2, 0.033 at.% from the row on each element. The samples are bulk single crystals measured with no applied pressure. Superconductivity is assigned to BaGa2 by the authors and is supported by a zero-resistance state, a diamagnetic susceptibility and a field-suppressed specific-heat jump whose size is a large fraction of gamma*Tc, which rules out a trace inclusion; the obvious flux-related impurity, alpha-Ga, would appear near 1.08 K and does not, and the growth flux was Ba-rich. Every contrary report I found (Haarmann et al. 2009 specific heat with no transition from 1.8 K; Hosono et al. 2015 survey listing BaGa2 among non-superconductors with no stated temperature; transport studies to 1.8-2 K) stops above 0.36 K, which explains the table's zeros without contradicting the 2022 measurement. No correction, comment or retraction was found, and the DOI is registered with Crossref. Remaining caveats (single group, no phase data in the 2022 paper itself, an unexplained chi' spike, a sub-BCS gap ratio, Meng et al. 2002 unread) are not reasons of substance against the label change. Apply: BaGa2 is a bulk ambient-pressure superconductor with Tc = 0.36 K.

reader_a.evidence_note: Read the full text of arXiv:2310.03818v2, the preprint of Phys. Rev. B 109, 104520 (2024), including the page images of Table I and Fig. 7. The STATED route is met by the two rapidly cooled samples of nominal MoB2: the ρ-bar sample is bulk, its resistivity falls to about zero on the scale of Fig. 7(a) with onset 4.45 K, and its specific heat shows an anomaly with Tc mid 4.08 K (Fig. 7(b)); the splat-quenched foil has a resistive onset at 4.55 K; the pressure is ambient. The published abstract, read through the FastTrack record of the DOI, carries the same claim (superconductivity in MoB2 at ambient pressure, critical temperature 4.5 K). Points of substance against applying the correction, which the sceptic should weigh: (a) the same paper reports a null for the same nominal composition made by ordinary arc melting: 'In the arc-melted MoB2, no superconductivity was observed down to 1.7 K' (Table I caption; also Conclusions). The result therefore depends on the cooling rate, and the current label is correct for arc-melted R-3m MoB2. (b) The authors hedge the composition: 'The lack of a clear match in the XRD results implies that the precise stoichiometry is uncertain. Our nominal composition is based solely on the ratios of the constituents'; they write that this 'may be the first observation of superconductivity in stoichiometric ambient pressure MoB2 if excess boron can be ruled out' and that the results 'potentially offer the first evidence'. Their argument against excess boron is only that the XRD pattern differs from that of MoB2.5. (c) The authors assume that about 50% of the ρ-bar sample is superconducting, and they do not identify the phase that superconducts. MoB2.5 (71.4 at.% B) is a known superconductor, so a boron-rich or defect phase as the superconducting part is not excluded by the paper. (d) The paper cites Cooper et al. 1970 as finding that splat-quenched MoB2 did not superconduct down to 1.8 K; that paper was not opened in this session. The verdict is 'confirmed' because the route fixed in advance is met by the paper's own text, table and figure; it is not a statement that equilibrium MoB2 superconducts.

sceptic.source_re_read: arXiv:2310.03818v2 (12 Oct 2023), the preprint of P. M. Dee et al., Phys. Rev. B 109, 104520 (2024). Opened at https://arxiv.org/pdf/2310.03818; text read with pdftotext and pages 5 to 7 (Table I, Fig. 6, Fig. 7, Section IV) viewed as page images. The published journal text was not opened.
sceptic.doi_check: FastTrack verify_reference: registered at Crossref, Physical Review B 109 (10), 104520 (2024), same title and the same ten authors as the arXiv paper. The arXiv abstract page lists this DOI. No retraction flagged; a Crossref search for an erratum returned only the article itself.
sceptic.what_the_readers_found_and_i_confirm: Both readers read the paper correctly. Table I (arXiv p. 5): 'MoB2 rho-bar' Tc onset 4.45 K, Tc mid 4.08 K, dC/(gamma Tc mid) 0.76, RRR 1.23; 'MoB2 w.c.s.q.' Tc onset 4.55 K, RRR 1.28; 'MoB2 (R-3m) a.m.' < 1.7 K, RRR 2.74. Fig. 7(a) (p. 6): the resistivity of both rapidly cooled samples falls to zero on the scale of the plot. Fig. 7(b): specific-heat anomaly of the rho-bar sample, Tc mid 4.08 K. Section IV (p. 7) and the Conclusions (p. 10) say the two rapidly cooled samples superconduct at ambient pressure. The arithmetic for the nominal formula holds: MoB2 = Mo 1/3 = 33.33 at.%, B 2/3 = 66.67 at.%; row Mo 33.3, B 66.7; difference 0.03 at.% on each element, inside 0.15 at.%. The sample is bulk (a cast bar of about 1 x 1 x 4 mm3) and no pressure was applied.
refutation_attempts: Composition. The 0.03 at.% agreement is with the weighed-in (nominal) formula only. The paper did not measure the composition of the superconducting samples and says so. Section IV: 'The lack of a clear match in the XRD results implies that the precise stoichiometry is uncertain. Our nominal composition is based solely on the ratios of the constituents used in the arc-melting process.' Discussion: 'Understanding the exact B:Mo ratio would provide crucial context for the significance of our findings.' So the at.% check cannot be made for the material that superconducts.

Does the superconductivity belong to the MoB2 phase or to another phase? Not settled by the paper. The authors condition their own claim: 'This may be the first observation of superconductivity in stoichiometric ambient pressure MoB2 if excess boron can be ruled out.' and in the Discussion their results 'potentially offer' the first evidence. From the specific-heat jump (0.76) they write 'we can assume that around 50% of the sample is superconducting', so about half of the bar is not superconducting. The XRD of the rho-bar sample has ill-defined peaks and no phase is assigned; the Table I caption says the space groups 'are likely to be R3̄m but remain unknown', and the text says the lowest-angle peak matches P6/mmm better. P6/mmm is the structure of the boron-rich MoB2.5 samples in the same paper, which superconduct with onsets of 3.06 K (arc-melted) and 5.82 K (rho-bar), on either side of the 4.45 K seen in nominal MoB2. The only argument offered against a boron-rich superconducting part is that the XRD pattern of MoB2.5 looks different; the authors call this 'helping to rule out' excess boron, not ruling it out. The rule excludes a multi-phase sample where the superconducting part is another compound; here that possibility is left open by the authors themselves.

Same composition, ordinary synthesis, same paper. The arc-melted sample of the same nominal MoB2 (XRD closest to R-3m, RRR 2.74) did not superconduct down to 1.7 K (Table I and its caption; Conclusions: 'our arc-melted MoB2 was not superconducting to 1.7 K'). The current label is therefore correct for MoB2 as it is normally made.

Earlier work with the same technique. I opened A. S. Cooper et al., Proc. Natl. Acad. Sci. 67, 313 (1970), DOI 10.1073/pnas.67.1.313 (PMC scan, text obtained by OCR through one Firecrawl PDF scrape). Its Table 3 lists two splat-melted samples of nominal MoB2 (nos. 9083 and 9408) as 'not superconducting', and a splat-melted nominal MoB2.5 (no. 9409) with Tc onset 8.1 K. Its text: 'Even a splat-melted MoB2, which is presumably the stoichiometric composition, did not have a large enough cell volume to become superconducting', and as-cast 'MoB2' 'is very close to MoB1.7'. So rapid quenching of nominal MoB2 gave a null in 1970 and a superconductor in 2023, and Cooper et al. tie superconductivity in this phase to extra boron and an expanded cell. This is a direct contrary report and it supports the reading that the actual boron content, not the nominal formula, decides the result.

Other measurements of MoB2 at ambient pressure. Hire et al., Phys. Rev. B 106, 174515 (2022), read as arXiv:2212.14869v1: 'MoB2 (R3̄m) showed no superconductivity, in agreement with the paper by Fisk [15].' (arc-melted, stoichiometric; I did not find the lowest temperature in the text). Lim et al., Phys. Rev. B 108, 094501 (2023), read as arXiv:2302.13936v2: 'At ambient pressure MoB2 exists in an R3m structure, which is non-superconducting at low pressure.' Pei et al. (arXiv:2105.13250, opened) is a pressure study of flux-grown R-3m crystals: the first small resistive drop appears at 21.7 GPa at Tmin 1.8 K; it makes no ambient-pressure claim either way.

Replication and follow-up. I found none. FastTrack get_citations for the DOI lists 9 citing works; by title and abstract snippet none measures quenched MoB2 or its composition. arXiv listing searches ('MoB2 superconductivity', 'MoB$_2$ superconductivity', 'MoB$_{2}$ superconductivity', 'MoB$_2$ ambient pressure', 'molybdenum diboride superconductivity', 'MoB2 quenched', 'diboride splat quenching superconductivity') returned no follow-up. A later paper from the same group that cites Dee et al., Sinha et al., arXiv:2408.17416 (opened), summarises that paper only for the Zr-, Hf- and Ta-substituted compounds and still describes superconductivity in pure MoB2 as first appearing near 21 GPa; it does not mention ambient-pressure superconductivity in quenched MoB2. Dee et al. themselves write that 'the precise composition and properties of rapidly cooled MoB2 under high pressure are the subject of future work'.

Kind of evidence. For MoB2 the paper gives resistivity (both rapidly cooled samples) and specific heat (rho-bar only). There are no magnetization data for MoB2. The specific-heat anomaly does show that the superconductivity in the bar is not a thin filament; it is a large fraction of the sample. It does not say which phase or composition carries it.
Bulk and pressure. No objection: the rho-bar sample is a bulk cast bar and the foil is a quenched melt, not a deposited film; measurements are at ambient pressure.

Version read. I read arXiv v2, not the journal text. The abstract in the journal's index record (FastTrack get_paper) ends with the same sentence on MoB2 and 4.5 K. Whether Section IV changed in review is unchecked.

Where the table's zeros may come from. The task file shows 2 zero reports from SuperCon. I could not open SuperCon. Candidates consistent with a zero: the two 'not superconducting' MoB2 rows of Cooper et al. 1970, Table 3 (read), and Leyarovska and Leyarovski, J. Less-Common Met. 67, 249 (1979), DOI 10.1016/0022-5088(79)90100-0 (Crossref-registered; paywalled, not read). This attribution is not established.

sceptic.verifier_reason: Do not apply. The readers' reading is accurate and the paper does state superconductivity (resistive onset 4.45 K, specific-heat midpoint 4.08 K) in a bulk, rapidly cooled bar of nominal MoB2 at ambient pressure. The doubt is one of substance and it comes from the paper itself: the composition and structure of the superconducting samples were not determined ('the precise stoichiometry is uncertain'), only about half of the bar superconducts, and the authors make their claim conditional on excess boron being ruled out, which they do not do. Boron-rich Mo-B samples are superconductors in the same temperature range in this paper (MoB2.5: 3.06 to 5.82 K) and in Cooper et al. 1970 (MoB2.5: 8.1 K onset), so a superconducting part with a composition other than the row's is a live explanation, and the rule does not count a multi-phase sample whose superconducting part may be another compound. Against the single positive report stand nulls for the same nominal composition that I read myself: the arc-melted sample of the same paper (to 1.7 K), two splat-melted samples of Cooper et al. 1970 (the same quenching idea, opposite result), and the arc-melted sample of Hire et al. 2022. I found no replication and no follow-up that fixes the composition. The row is a composition label; for MoB2 as normally made the current label is supported by several measurements, and the one positive result is for a metastable, unidentified material whose actual composition is unknown. That is not enough to say this composition superconducts.

reader_a.source_url: https://spiral.imperial.ac.uk/bitstreams/957cc4bc-062d-49c5-b7eb-3c1e1e068bbc/download (thesis PDF; item page http://hdl.handle.net/10044/1/17504)

Fig. 15, p. 124 carries the curve labelled 17.1 at.% Tl. Phase statements: p. 70 and section 4.24, p. 154.
reader_a.tc_criterion: A.c. induction (mutual inductance) signal against temperature; Tc is the average, for heating and cooling, of the temperature at half the amplitude change (midpoint). Transition breadth 0.18 K.
reader_a.pressure: ambient: the thesis describes no pressure apparatus; the specimens sat in wax blocks in a helium cryostat and temperatures below 4.2 K were reached by pumping on the helium bath (pp. 67, 72-74). The thesis does not use the word 'ambient'.
reader_a.measurement_method: A.c. induction at 700 c/s with a field of 0.24 gauss at the specimens, pick-up coil signal displayed on an oscilloscope, germanium resistance thermometer calibrated against a standardised germanium thermometer (pp. 65-67, 73-78).
reader_a.synthesis_conditions: Spectrographically standardised In and Tl. A 100 g master alloy with 36 at.% Tl was melted under half an atmosphere of argon in sealed Pyrex at 350 C, chill cast into ice/water, homogenised 48 h at 140 C and extruded to 2 mm wire. Five-gram ingots of each composition were made the same way in 5 mm i.d. tubes from the master alloy and pure indium and annealed at 145 C for 24 h immediately before examination (pp. 52-53). Tc was measured within a few hours of quenching from the annealing temperature (p. 123).

Taken together, a sample 0.6 at.% below (with a Tc) and a sample 1.0 at.% above (superconducting at 2.29 K, no Tc) bracket 25.0 at.% Tl. Rev. 168, 715-725 (1968), DOI 10.1103/PhysRev.168.715: look at the table of Zr-Ti alloys (composition, gamma, Debye temperature, Tc) and the Tc-versus-composition figure; the calorimeter floor was 1.1 K, so an alloy listed without a Tc was normal down to about 1.1 K.

tasks.lane: backlog: a paper that could settle rows cycle 3 could not read

reader_a.paper_formula: Ba1-xKxBiO3 with x = 0.25 (Ba0.75K0.25BiO3), as written in Shang et al. 2020; the task's named paper (Hinks et al. 1988) writes Ba1-xKxBiO3-y and its abstract gives no sample at x = 0.25
reader_a.at_pct_check: Ba0.75K0.25BiO3 has 0.75 + 0.25 + 1 + 3 = 5 atoms. Ba 0.75/5 = 0.150, K 0.25/5 = 0.050, Bi 1/5 = 0.200, O 3/5 = 0.600. Row: Ba 0.150, K 0.050, Bi 0.200, O 0.600. Difference 0.00 at.% on every element, so the paper's x = 0.25 sample is the row composition. Neighbours in the same series: x = 0.20 is Ba 16.0, K 4.0 at.% (1.0 at.% from the row on Ba and on K); x = 0.30 is Ba 14.0, K 6.0 at.% (1.0 at.% from the row).
reader_a.phase_or_sample: Polycrystalline sample made by solid-state reaction. The authors say their Rietveld refinements show that samples with 0.1 <= x <= 0.25 are a mixture of orthorhombic and cubic phases. Superconducting fraction of the x = 0.25 sample: below 1%. The authors call only x = 0.3 to 0.6 bulk superconductors.
reader_a.source_url: https://arxiv.org/pdf/1912.12112 (v2, 15 Jan 2020; the arXiv record gives journal reference Phys. Rev. B 101, 014508 (2020) and the same DOI)
reader_a.page_table_or_figure: arXiv v2 page 2, Section III 'Characterization of bulk superconductivity' (left column), and Fig. 1(c) on the same page; page 1, Introduction, for the phase-mixture statement and for 'x = 0.3-0.6 show bulk superconductivity'. Page numbers are those of the arXiv version, not the journal.
reader_a.tc_criterion: Not applicable. The paper mentions a transition at 25 K in ZFC/FC dc susceptibility (1 mT) for x = 0.25, with a superconducting fraction below 1%; it is not given as a bulk Tc, and Fig. 1(c) plots the x = 0.25 susceptibility point at T = 0.
reader_a.pressure: Not stated in words. Magnetic susceptibility was measured in a Quantum Design MPMS in a 1 mT field; no pressure cell is mentioned, so this is an ordinary ambient-pressure measurement.
reader_a.measurement_method: dc magnetic susceptibility, zero-field-cooled and field-cooled, 1 mT, Quantum Design MPMS (also muon-spin rotation for x = 0.3, 0.4, 0.6 only)
reader_a.synthesis_conditions: Polycrystalline, solid-state reaction; details are in the paper's Supplementary Material, which I did not open. Atomic ratios were measured by x-ray fluorescence.
reader_a.bracket_samples: Same series (Shang et al. 2020). Low side: 'x <= 0.2' (x = 0.20 is K 4.0 at.%, 1.0 at.% from the row): no superconducting transition down to 1.8 K. High side: x = 0.30 (K 6.0 at.%, 1.0 at.% from the row): bulk superconductor, Tc = 29.5 K. The bracket fails: the low-side neighbour does not superconduct, and the authors say the samples with 0.1 <= x <= 0.25 are not single phase.
reader_a.quote: For x ≤ 0.2, no superconducting transition could be detected down to 1.8 K. For x = 0.25, the χ(T) curve shows a superconducting transition at 25 K with a rather small superconducting fraction (below 1%).
reader_a.evidence_note: Deciding source read in full: Shang et al., arXiv:1912.12112v2 = Phys. Rev. B 101, 014508 (2020). It measured a polycrystalline x = 0.25 sample and reports only a trace transition (fraction below 1%) at 25 K in a sample the authors describe as a mixture of orthorhombic and cubic phases. In Fig. 1(c) the susceptibility markers of this work sit on the T = 0 line at x = 0.10, 0.15, 0.20 and 0.25, and the superconducting region starts at x = 0.3. The introduction says the samples 'with x = 0.3–0.6 show bulk superconductivity'. So this paper does not report Ba0.75K0.25BiO3 as a bulk superconductor. The task's named paper, Hinks et al., Nature 333, 836 (1988), doi 10.1038/333836a0: I could read only its abstract (from the SciSpace record). The abstract says superconductivity 'occurs only in a cubic perovskite phase ... which forms only for x > 0.25' and that Tc 'is highest for compositions near the structural phase transition (x ≈ 0.25)'. It gives no Tc for a sample at x = 0.25 and places x = 0.25 at the edge of, not inside, the superconducting phase. Later work by the same group moves the edge higher. Pei et al., Phys. Rev. B 41, 4126 (1990), abstract only: 'Bulk superconductivity occurs only in a cubic perovskite phase which exists for x≥0.37 (at 10 K)'. Hinks et al. 1990 (OSTI report CONF-900206--7, the preprint of J. Less-Common Met. 168, 19 (1991), doi 10.1016/0022-5088(91)90031-X), text read in full: 'the material remains semiconducting to a potassium concentration of 0.375'. That sentence is a general statement about the series, not a measurement reported for an x = 0.25 sample. One abstract does state a null for this composition: Misra et al., Phys. Rev. B 53, 9442 (1996), doi 10.1103/PhysRevB.53.9442, speaks of 'the two nonsuperconducting specimens characterized by the smaller concentrations x̄=0.13, 0.25' (x̄ is the analysed potassium content) (ceramics; EPR and microwave absorption at 4-100 K; x from chemical analysis with an uncertainty of ±0.03). I did not give verified_null on it; the reasons are in reason_if_not.
reader_a.reason_if_not: Not confirmed as a superconductor: no source I opened states bulk superconductivity with a Tc for Ba0.75K0.25BiO3. The one full text that measures x = 0.25 (Shang et al. 2020) reports a transition at 25 K with a superconducting fraction below 1% in a two-phase sample, which the owner's rule does not count (not bulk; multi-phase sample), and the authors themselves plot that sample at T = 0 and call only x = 0.3-0.6 bulk superconductors. The bracketed route fails because the low-side neighbour (x <= 0.2) shows no transition down to 1.8 K and the low-x samples are not single phase. The named Nature paper could not be opened beyond its abstract, which gives no Tc at x = 0.25. Not given verified_null either: Shang et al. do report a (trace) transition for x = 0.25 rather than its absence, and state the 1.8 K limit only for x <= 0.2. The Misra et al. 1996 null was read as an abstract only, its stated composition uncertainty (±0.03 in x, which is ±0.6 at.% K) is wider than the 0.15 at.% limit, the abstract hints that the low-x specimens contain a Ba0.875K0.125BiO3 phase, and it does not say in one sentence that no superconductivity was seen down to 4 K. Everything read points to the present label (not a superconductor) being right, but the strict wording for a verified null is not met by text I read.
reader_a.leads_for_library: 1) Hinks et al., Nature 333, 836-838 (1988), doi 10.1038/333836a0: check the sample list and the Tc-versus-x figure or text for whether a sample at x = 0.25 was measured and what Tc, if any, is given. 2) Pei et al., Phys. Rev. B 41, 4126 (1990), doi 10.1103/PhysRevB.41.4126: the phase diagram figure and the sample table; look for an x = 0.25 sample and the lowest temperature of its susceptibility test. 3) Misra et al., Phys. Rev. B 53, 9442-9447 (1996), doi 10.1103/PhysRevB.53.9442: the full text should say how the x = 0.25 specimen was shown to be non-superconducting and down to what temperature; that could support a verified null. 4) Pei, Zheng, Hinks et al., 'Structure and transport properties of melt processed Ba1-xKxBiO3' (1990), open access at the UNT Digital Library, ark:/67531/metadc1207117: resistivity of single-phase samples across 0 < x < 0.5; its abstract says bulk superconductors only for x > 0.35. 5) Supplementary Material of Phys. Rev. B 101, 014508 (2020): measured XRF composition and the susceptibility curve of the x = 0.25 sample.

reader_a.page_table_or_figure: p. 1151, last two paragraphs (text on Fig. 1); p. 1152, Fig. 1 (Ce point) and Fig. 2 (resistance of Y0.96Ce0.04B6); p. 1153, first two paragraphs. The paper has no table.
reader_a.pressure: Not stated in the paper. Nothing in it mentions applied pressure for the YB6 samples.
reader_a.measurement_method: Not stated for the transition temperatures behind Fig. 1. Fig. 2 is an electrical resistance measurement.
reader_a.synthesis_conditions: Not stated in the paper.
reader_a.bracket_samples: No usable bracket. The paper does not list the concentrations of the samples behind Fig. 1; the ordinate is a rate, '-dTc (K per %)'. The only cerium sample with a stated composition is Y0.96Ce0.04B6 (Ce 0.571 at.%, 0.47 at.% from the row along the series), and Fig. 2 shows its resistance from about 1.6 K to about 35 K with no superconducting transition. On the other side is the host YB6 (Ce 0 at.%, 0.10 at.% from the row in Ce), for which this paper gives no Tc.
reader_a.quote: Figure 1 shows the depression of the superconducting transition temperature of YB6 with 1 atomic per cent addition of rare earth for Y.
reader_a.evidence_note: I read all four pages of Fisk, Matthias and Corenzwit, PNAS 64, 1151-1154 (1969), from the scanned page images on PubMed Central. Fig. 1 plots the depression of the superconducting transition temperature of YB6 per atomic per cent of rare earth substituted for Y. The Ce point reads 0.81 K per at.% (my digitisation of the figure; the Gd point reads 1.58 on the same scale). The text calls this a 'large effect of Ce additions' compared with the trend of the other rare earths. A depression of this size means that YB6 with about 1 at.% Ce on the Y site was still superconducting in these authors' samples. The paper does not give a transition temperature anywhere, neither for YB6 nor for any doped sample, and does not list which concentrations were measured. A Tc for the row could only be derived by subtracting about 0.8 K from a YB6 value taken from another paper; that is my inference, not a statement of this paper. Fig. 2 shows that Y0.96Ce0.04B6 has a resistance minimum near 16-17 K and a resistance that rises on cooling and flattens near 1.6-2 K, with no superconducting transition over the plotted range (about 1.6 K to 35 K); the paper does not comment on superconductivity of that sample. If YB6 itself has a Tc of about 6 K or more (6.0 K in the Cornell report cited below; this paper gives no value), a linear 0.81 K per at.% rate would leave a Tc near 2.8 K at 4 at.%, above the 1.6 K reached in Fig. 2; so the Fig. 1 rate cannot be extended linearly to 4 at.%. A second group appears to report a much stronger effect. The final report of the Cornell grant (DTIC ADA065668, 1979), summarising Sobczak and Sienko's paper then in press, says YB6 powder had Tc 6.0 K, that 0.3% iron lowered it to 3.3 K, and: 'A smaller amount of cerium than iron lowered the Tc value more.' It gives no cerium concentration and no Tc for a cerium sample, and it does not define its '%'. Read at face value, less than 0.3% Ce lowering Tc by more than 2.7 K is a rate above 9 K per %, more than ten times the 0.81 K per at.% of Fig. 1. I read that report as OCR text and treat it as a lead, not as the paper. The two sources therefore appear to disagree on how strongly Ce depresses Tc in YB6, and nothing I opened states a Tc, or a null result with a temperature, for the row's composition.
reader_a.reason_if_not: Route STATED fails on 'with a Tc': the paper gives only a depression rate (about 0.8 K per at.% Ce for Y) and no transition temperature for any sample, and it does not say that a sample at this composition was the one measured. Route BRACKETED fails: the measured concentrations are not listed, and the one cerium sample with a stated composition (Y0.96Ce0.04B6) shows no superconductivity down to about 1.6 K in Fig. 2. It is not a verified null either: no source I read says this composition was measured and found not to superconduct. The second primary paper that examined Ce in YB6 (Sobczak and Sienko 1979) is paywalled and was not read.
reader_a.leads_for_library: 1) R. J. Sobczak and M. J. Sienko, 'Superconductivity in the hexaborides', J. Less-Common Metals 67 (1979) 167-171, DOI 10.1016/0022-5088(79)90088-2: look for the table or figure of Tc against impurity content for (Y,Ce)B6, the cerium concentrations, the Tc values and the lowest temperature reached. This is the paper most likely to settle the row either way. 2) B. T. Matthias et al., Science 159, 530 (1968), DOI 10.1126/science.159.3814.530: the Tc of YB6 from the laboratory that made the Fig. 1 samples (not opened here). 3) The PNAS paper has no sample table; a thesis by its first author from the same period, if one exists, may tabulate the Fig. 1 samples (not checked). 4) B. W. Roberts, NBS Technical Note 724 (1972), DOI 10.6028/nbs.tn.724, cites the PNAS paper and may show how this entry reached the databases (secondary, not opened). 5) Outside this task: the training table's neighbouring row B:0.857;Ce:0.007;Y:0.136 (Y0.95Ce0.05B6, labelled superconductor, 1.6 K) is not supported by anything I read; Fig. 2 of the PNAS paper shows Y0.96Ce0.04B6 without a transition down to about 1.6 K. It may deserve its own check.

reader_a.paper_formula: Named paper (Ricci et al., SuST 24, 082002): nominal K0.8Fe1.6Se2; measured (EDX) K:Fe:Se = 0.6:1.5:2. Companion paper (Ricci et al., PRB 84, 060511(R)) gives EDX K:Fe:Se = 0.8:1.6:2 for a crystal with Tc = 31.8 K.
reader_a.at_pct_check: Row = K0.8Fe1.6Se2 exactly: K 0.8/4.4 = 18.18, Fe 1.6/4.4 = 36.36, Se 2/4.4 = 45.45 at.%. (1) The SuST paper's measured composition, K0.6Fe1.5Se2: total 4.1, so K 14.63, Fe 36.59, Se 48.78 at.%. Differences: K -3.55, Fe +0.22, Se +3.33 at.%. This FAILS the 0.15 at.% limit. The same 0.6:1.5:2 EDX result and the 31.8 K zero-resistance Tc appear in Mizuguchi et al. APL 98, 042511, the paper the SuST text cites for its Tc. (2) The PRB companion's EDX value, K0.8Fe1.6Se2, matches the row exactly (differences 0.00 at.%), but it is the average over a two-phase crystal (see phase_or_sample). (3) Carr et al. PRB 89, 134509 split a superconducting crystal of average composition K0.76Fe1.64Se2 (K 17.27, Fe 37.27, Se 45.45; K -0.91, Fe +0.91 at.%, fails) into two phases. One is insulating K0.798Fe1.59Se2: K 18.19, Fe 36.24, Se 45.58, i.e. within 0.13 at.% of the row, and it is the NON-superconducting block-AF phase. The other is superconducting K0.53Fe2Se2: K 11.70, Fe 44.15, Se 44.15, i.e. 6-8 at.% away. (4) Wang et al. EPL 111, 27004 call their bulk superconductor K1.9Fe4.2Se5: K 17.12, Fe 37.84, Se 45.05. Differences: K -1.06, Fe +1.47, Se -0.41 at.%, which fails.
reader_a.phase_or_sample: Bulk single crystals grown from the melt (FeSe precursor + K), studied with synchrotron XRD in transmission. The named paper reports intrinsic phase separation below 520 K into two phases. The majority phase (about 79% at 350 K) is magnetic, with a ThCr2Si2-type lattice modulated by sqrt5 x sqrt5 Fe-vacancy order. The minority phase is non-magnetic, with a compressed in-plane lattice and a weak sqrt2 x sqrt2 superstructure. The paper's discussion pairs a majority magnetic phase (5x5 ordered defects) with a superconducting phase (the second, 2x2 superstructure) of different charge density. So the superconducting part is assigned to the minority phase, not to the vacancy-ordered phase. The PRB companion reports the same split: phase A, expanded and vacancy-ordered, magnetic; phase B, 2.5% shorter a, non-magnetic, about 20-30% by volume.
reader_a.source_url: https://arxiv.org/pdf/1107.0409 (arXiv version of the named SuST paper); also opened https://arxiv.org/pdf/1107.0412 (PRB 84, 060511), https://arxiv.org/pdf/1012.4950 (APL 98, 042511), https://arxiv.org/pdf/1404.3715 (PRB 89, 134509), https://arxiv.org/pdf/1502.01116 (EPL 111, 27004), https://arxiv.org/pdf/1311.0492 (PRB 88, 184413)
reader_a.page_table_or_figure: SuST arXiv 1107.0409: Experimental section (p. 2) for composition and Tc source; Results/Fig. 3 for the phase fractions; Discussion (p. 5) for which phase superconducts. PRB arXiv 1107.0412: experimental paragraph (p. 2) gives EDX 0.8:1.6:2 and Tc = 31.8 K; Fig. 2 and the text after it give the A/B phases and the B fraction of about 20-30%.
reader_a.tc_criterion: Reported for the crystal, not confirmed for this composition. In Mizuguchi et al. APL 98, 042511 (cited as Ref. [4] in the SuST paper), Tc zero = 31.8 K and Tc onset = 33.0 K come from resistivity, on the crystal whose EDX composition is K:Fe:Se = 0.6:1.5:2. The PRB companion states Tc = 31.8 K and a sharp transition at about 32 K from SQUID magnetization and four-probe resistivity.
reader_a.pressure: ambient (no pressure applied in any of the papers read)
reader_a.measurement_method: The named paper measures structure only (temperature-dependent single-crystal synchrotron XRD, 80-600 K). Its Tc comes from resistivity and magnetization reported in Ref. [4] (Mizuguchi et al.). The PRB companion cites SQUID magnetization and four-probe resistivity.
reader_a.synthesis_conditions: From the PRB companion: FeSe precursor and K (nominal ratio 2:0.8) melted in an alumina crucible sealed in a stainless-steel tube; 1030 C for 2 h, then slow cooling to 750 C at 6 C/h; plate-like crystals.
reader_a.quote: The actual composition of the crystal was estimated to be K:Fe:Se=0.6:1.5:2 using an average of four points of the EDX measurements. The resistivity and magnetization studies showed the presence of a sharp superconducting transition at about 31.8 K (Tc onset 33 K) [4].
reader_a.evidence_note: Neither route is met. STATED fails for the named paper on three counts. (a) Its measured composition, K0.6Fe1.5Se2, is 3.5 at.% off on K and 3.3 at.% off on Se. (b) The Tc is not measured in this paper; it is cited from Mizuguchi et al. (APL 98, 042511), who give the same EDX 0.6:1.5:2 result and Tc zero = 31.8 K for their crystal. (c) The paper's own phase analysis shows a two-phase crystal: a majority (about 79%) vacancy-ordered magnetic phase plus a minority compressed phase, and the discussion pairs superconductivity with the minority phase ('a majority magnetic metallic phase with 5x5 ordered defects and a superconducting phase with a second 2x2 superstructure order with different charge densities'). The PRB companion (10.1103/PhysRevB.84.060511) does state EDX K:Fe:Se = 0.8:1.6:2, an exact match, and Tc = 31.8 K. But that composition is the average of the same two-phase crystal (A phase vacancy-ordered and magnetic; B phase compressed, non-magnetic, about 20-30%). The two Ricci papers also disagree on the crystal's EDX composition (0.6:1.5:2 vs 0.8:1.6:2) for what both describe as the Tc = 31.8 K crystal. Two later primary papers bear directly on which phase superconducts. Carr et al. PRB 89, 134509 (2014), neutron Rietveld plus ICP: a superconducting crystal (Tc about 32 K, average K0.76Fe1.64Se2) separates into insulating K0.798Fe1.59Se2, which lies within 0.13 at.% of this row, and superconducting K0.53Fe2Se2; a crystal grown at nominal K0.8Fe1.6Se2 (refined K0.78Fe1.58Se2) stays single-phase and insulating. Wang et al. EPL 111, 27004 (2015): stoichiometric K2Fe4Se5 polycrystals are non-superconducting as grown and after a 300 C anneal. After a 750 C anneal and quench, the same composition shows only 'superconducting-like' diamagnetic transitions (29 or 31 K, and 11 K) with low volume fraction and semiconducting resistivity, described as 'disconnected superconducting puddles'. Bulk superconductivity there appears only at K1.9Fe4.2Se5, about 1.5 at.% Fe away. Under the owner's rule this is a multi-phase sample in which the superconducting part is another compound (Fe-rich, K-poor KzFe2Se2), and the phase at this row's composition is the insulating 245 phase. That is not a confirmation. verified_null is also not met by what I read. Carr's insulating crystal (K0.78Fe1.58Se2) is 0.42 at.% off on Se, and its lowest transport temperature is not stated in the text. Nandi et al. PRB 88, 184413 call their K0.8Fe1.6Se2 crystal 'non-superconducting' but report no low-temperature superconductivity test. Wang et al.'s nominal K2Fe4Se5 gives a trace superconducting signal after the 750 C treatment.
reader_a.reason_if_not: No primary paper read states bulk superconductivity of a single phase at K0.8Fe1.6Se2 (within 0.15 at.%). The named paper's measured composition is K0.6Fe1.5Se2 (3.5 at.% off), and its Tc is cited from another paper. Where the exact composition is reported (Ricci PRB EDX 0.8:1.6:2), it is the average of a phase-separated crystal whose superconductivity the same group assigns to the minority compressed phase. Carr et al. (2014) identify the phase at this composition, K0.798Fe1.59Se2, as the insulating block-AF phase and the superconducting phase as K0.53Fe2Se2. The rule excludes multi-phase samples where the superconducting part is another compound. No single-phase bracketing series exists: superconducting KxFe2-ySe2 samples are phase-separated, and Wang et al.'s single-phase K2-xFe4+ySe5 series reaches bulk superconductivity only at K1.9Fe4.2Se5, about 1.5 at.% away on one side, with no superconducting sample on the other side.
reader_a.leads_for_library: (1) Ricci et al., Supercond. Sci. Technol. 24, 082002 (2011), doi:10.1088/0953-2048/24/8/082002: Experimental section and Discussion. Read here from arXiv:1107.0409; the published version may differ. (2) Ricci et al., PRB 84, 060511(R) (2011), doi:10.1103/PhysRevB.84.060511: experimental paragraph (EDX 0.8:1.6:2, Tc 31.8 K). (3) Mizuguchi et al., APL 98, 042511 (2011), doi:10.1063/1.3549702: EDX 0.6:1.5:2, Tc onset 33.0 K, Tc zero 31.8 K. (4) Carr et al., PRB 89, 134509 (2014), doi:10.1103/PhysRevB.89.134509: summary (insulating K0.798Fe1.59Se2 plus superconducting K0.53Fe2Se2) and Fig. 2. (5) Wang C.-H. et al., EPL 111, 27004 (2015), doi:10.1209/0295-5075/111/27004: Fig. 1(a) and Fig. 3(a) for K2Fe4Se5 in its as-grown, 300 C-annealed and 750 C-quenched states. A person could check the Fig. 1(a) temperature range to see whether the as-grown and 300 C-annealed K2Fe4Se5 give a verified_null. (6) Nandi et al., PRB 88, 184413 (2013), doi:10.1103/PhysRevB.88.184413: 'non-superconducting K0.8Fe1.6Se2'; the low-temperature test is not shown in the text.

Bulk or film: both samples are bulk. One was arc-melted, the other ball-milled and spark-plasma-sintered. Neither is a film or a nanostructure. The abstract also presents the work as bearing on bulk superconductivity.

Pressure: the abstract mentions no applied pressure. The measurements it describes (resistivity, isothermal magnetization at 2 K, specific heat) are routine bulk measurements, so I take the pressure as ambient.

Phase purity and impurity superconductivity: the main risk is that the SPS sample contains Fe-bearing impurity phases from the stainless-steel milling media. The Kitagawa/Mizuguchi/Nishizaki review (arXiv 2504.06454, sections 3.2, 3.6 and 8; full text read via alphaXiv) says so, but these impurities are not superconductors that could explain the transition. For the arc-melted sample, the review mentions no impurity phase. The abstract's specific-heat jump of 3.3 at Tc for the AM sample is a bulk thermodynamic signal; a minority phase could not produce it. The AM Tc of 7.99 K is well below free Nb (about 9.2 K), so the transition is not from unreacted Nb. Senga et al. (arXiv 2602.19376, Table 2; full text read) list Nb2/5Hf1/5Zr1/5Ti1/5 among bcc alloys with Tc 7.99 K, theta_D 193 K and gamma 5.937 mJ/mol K^2, citing this paper. That is a secondary source and context only. The XRD figure of the primary paper was not read.

Family context (not bracketing, which needs neighbours within 2 at.%): equimolar TiZrNbHf (Nb 25 at.%) is reported as a single-phase bcc superconductor at about 6.0 to 6.3 K by Kosuth et al. 2024 (Low Temp. Phys. 50, 663), Sang et al. 2025 (single crystals, SuST 38, 055022) and Uporov et al. (as summarised in the review). Nb0.67(TiZrHf)0.33 is reported as a bulk bcc superconductor (Sobota and Bartz 2026, Materials). I read these only as search abstracts. Nb 40 at.% lies between them, and nothing in the family points to a non-superconducting window there.

reader_a.paper_formula: Not given in what I read. The abstract of Claeson, Luo and Merriam (1966) says only that Cd-Hg alloys 'covering the complete composition range' were measured. It names no sample at or near Hg90Cd10 and gives no Tc for one.
reader_a.at_pct_check: Row: Cd 10.0 at.%, Hg 90.0 at.%. The abstract gives these phase limits. Cd dissolves in Hg up to 1.5 +/- 0.25 at.% Cd at 193 K. The omega phase ends at 88 +/- 1 at.% Hg (Cd 11 to 13 at.%) at 193 K. The row's 10.0 at.% Cd is 8.5 at.% above the Hg(Cd) limit and about 2.0 at.% (1 to 3 at.%) below the omega boundary. At 193 K it therefore lies in the two-phase field, Hg(Cd) solid solution plus omega. STATED route: no sample within 0.15 at.% of Cd 10.0 / Hg 90.0 was seen in any source I read. BRACKETED route: no single-phase series can bracket the row, because it sits in a two-phase field. In de Haas and de Boer (1932), the only other primary paper I read in full, the measured samples nearest the row are pure Hg (Cd 0) and Cd 30 at.%. They are 10.0 and 20.0 at.% away, well beyond the 2 at.% limit.
reader_a.phase_or_sample: Sample details for this composition are unknown, because the full text was not read. Going by the abstract's own phase boundaries, Hg90Cd10 is a two-phase Hg(Cd) + omega alloy at 193 K. If it superconducts near the Hg transition (about 4 K), that superconductivity would belong to the Hg-rich terminal solid solution, which is another phase. de Haas and de Boer (1932) measured only Cd 30, 40 and 50 at.% rods; they treated these as Hg-lattice mixed crystals, a phase picture that the 1966 paper's omega-phase boundaries supersede.
reader_a.source_url: https://doi.org/10.1103/physrev.141.412 (abstract via OpenAlex get_work and FastTrack get_paper; full text closed). Also read in full: https://dwc.knaw.nl/DL/publications/PU00016201.pdf (de Haas and de Boer, Proc. KNAW 1932, Comm. Leiden 220a, via Firecrawl scrape, 4 pages).
reader_a.page_table_or_figure: Claeson et al. 1966: abstract only, pp. 412-418 not seen. de Haas and de Boer 1932: section 2, Tables I-III and Fig. 3 (samples at Cd 30, 40 and 50 at.%; pure Hg taken from earlier work).
reader_a.pressure: Not stated in the abstract. Not established for this composition.
reader_a.measurement_method: Not known for this sample. The 1966 abstract mentions measured normal-state resistivity. de Haas and de Boer used resistance measurements in liquid helium, but not on this composition.
reader_a.synthesis_conditions: Unknown for this composition. The 1966 abstract gives its phase boundaries at 193 K, which implies anneals at that temperature, but no sample history is stated.
reader_a.bracket_samples: None qualify. de Haas and de Boer 1932: pure Hg (Cd 0, Tc about 4.2 K, from earlier Leiden work), 10.0 at.% from the row; Cd 30 at.% (Tc 2.16 K, resistive), 20.0 at.% from the row. Both exceed 2 at.%, and the two-phase field from Cd about 1.5 to 12 at.% (Claeson et al. abstract) lies between them, so the series is not single-phase across the row.
reader_a.quote: The superconducting transition temperatures of Cd-Hg alloys covering the complete composition range have been determined.
reader_a.evidence_note: Claeson, Luo and Merriam, Phys. Rev. 141, 412 (1966), DOI registered with Crossref. The abstract was read, but OpenAlex marks the paper closed access and no open copy was found. The abstract lists Cd solubility in Hg as 1.5 +/- 0.25 at.% and the omega-phase boundary as 88 +/- 1 at.% Hg, both at 193 K, so the row lies in the Hg(Cd) + omega two-phase field. de Haas and de Boer, 'The Supraconductivity of Hg-Cd Alloys' (Proc. KNAW, 1932), was read in full: its quote is 'We measured the change of the resistance at the temperatures of liquid helium for mixed crystals, containing a percentage 30,40 and 50 atoms of Cd'. It has no sample near Cd 10 at.%. Webb, Marsiglio and Hirsch, arXiv:1502.04724, a review and so a secondary source, says only that HgCd alloys were found superconducting at Leiden in 1913 (Comm. Leiden 133a-d) and gives no compositions.
reader_a.reason_if_not: No source I could open states superconductivity for Cd 10.0 / Hg 90.0 at.% (within 0.15 at.%). The named 1966 paper is paywalled, and its abstract names no sample at this composition and gives no Tc for one. The abstract's phase boundaries put the composition in a two-phase Hg(Cd) + omega field, so the bracketed route cannot apply. Any superconductivity of such a sample near 4 K would most likely belong to the Hg-rich solid solution, which is another phase and is excluded by the rule. The 1932 Leiden series has no sample within 2 at.%. No paper read reports this composition as non-superconducting either, so verified_null does not apply.
reader_a.leads_for_library: 1) Claeson, Luo and Merriam, Phys. Rev. 141, 412-418 (1966), doi:10.1103/PhysRev.141.412. Check the sample/Tc table and the Tc-versus-composition figure for any sample with Cd 8-12 at.% (Hg 88-92 at.%): its anneal, its phase (two-phase Hg(Cd) + omega or single omega), its Tc and how Tc was defined, and whether a transition near 4 K is assigned to the Hg-rich phase. Also check how SuperCon's Tc = 0 for Cd0.1Hg0.9 could arise from this paper. 2) T. Claeson, Chalmers doctoral thesis (1967), 'Superconductivity of binary alloys based on mercury, thallium, lead, and bismuth', probably the same data in fuller form. 3) Phase diagram: Gumiński and Zabdyr, J. Phase Equilib. 13 (1992), doi:10.1007/BF02674986 (secondary). 4) Compilation lead: B. W. Roberts, NBS Technical Note 724 (1972), doi:10.6028/NBS.TN.724, Cd-Hg entries (secondary). 5) H. Kamerlingh Onnes, Comm. Leiden 133a-d (1913), early HgCd amalgam measurements; composition unknown.

reader_a.paper_formula: Bi2OS2 ("undoped Bi2OS2", HP annealed at 2 GPa / 470 C / 1 h, and HP synthesized at 470 C / 2 GPa / 1 h)
reader_a.at_pct_check: Bi2OS2 has 5 atoms: Bi 2/5 = 0.400, O 1/5 = 0.200, S 2/5 = 0.400. Row: Bi 0.400, O 0.200, S 0.400. Difference 0.000 on every element (limit 0.0015). The formula is nominal; the paper did not analyse the actual composition of the HP-annealed sample.
reader_a.phase_or_sample: Polycrystalline bulk. Fig. 4(a) XRD: Bi2OS2 main phase indexed to P4/nmm; HP-annealed a = 3.963(1) A, c = 13.794(3) A with small Bi metal and BN peaks ('constituent phases were almost unchanged'); HP-synthesized a = 3.964(2) A, c = 13.786(5) A with more impurities (Bi2S3, Bi). The as-synthesized (ambient, 300 C) sample of the same composition has a = 3.961(1) A, c = 13.808(2) A.
reader_a.source_url: https://arxiv.org/pdf/1508.01656 (arXiv preprint of the JPSJ paper; arXiv metadata gives DOI 10.7566/JPSJ.84.084703)
reader_a.page_table_or_figure: arXiv v1 Sec. 3.3, pp. 4-5; Fig. 4(b) (ZFC 4piM/H vs T, page 12); Fig. 6 (Tc onset(mag) vs lattice parameters, page 14). Ambient-pressure measurement after HP annealing stated in Sec. 1, p. 2.
reader_a.tc_criterion: Magnetic: kink in ZFC magnetization (2 Oe) at 1.8 K below which large diamagnetism appears (HP-annealed); plotted as Tc onset(mag) = 1.8 K in Fig. 6. HP-synthesized sample: large diamagnetism below 2.1 K (Fig. 6: 2.1 K). Authors: 'Tc of bulk superconductivity ... ~2 K'. A small ~4 K onset is attributed by the authors to an impurity phase such as Bi3O2S3.
reader_a.pressure: ambient during measurement. Sec. 1: 'In HP annealing, the as-synthesized samples undergo heat treatment in HP synthesis apparatus and physical properties are measured under ambient pressure.' The sample was processed at 2 GPa and 470 C beforehand.
reader_a.measurement_method: DC magnetization, SQUID magnetometer (Quantum Design MPMS) with iHelium3 insert down to 0.47 K; ZFC at 2 Oe for HP-annealed and HP-synthesized samples (FC/ZFC inset for HP-synthesized); 200 Oe for the as-synthesized sample.
reader_a.synthesis_conditions: Bi2OS2 by solid-state reaction at 300 C for ~100 h in an evacuated quartz ampoule; HP annealing of that sample at 2 GPa, 470 C, 1 h in a cubic-anvil apparatus (BN pressure medium). HP synthesis from Bi2O3 + Bi2S3 at 470 C, 2 GPa, 1 h.
reader_a.quote: In contrast, HP annealed Bi2OS2 showed superconductivity. The onset of diamagnetic transition is ~4 K, a kink in ZFC curve is at 1.8 K and large diamagnetism is observed below this temperature.
reader_a.evidence_note: The paper states superconductivity of Bi2OS2 (exact composition) in a bulk polycrystalline sample measured at ambient pressure: HP-annealed Bi2OS2 reaches 4piM/H of about -1.6 at 0.47 K in Fig. 4(b), and the text concludes 'These results suggest that the Tc of bulk superconductivity for the HP annealed / synthesized samples are ~2 K.' The rule's exclusions do not name samples processed under pressure and measured at ambient, so I read route STATED as met. Two facts the sceptic and owner should weigh: (1) the same paper reports the ambient-synthesized Bi2OS2 as non-superconducting: 'This apparently indicates that as-synthesized undoped Bi2OS2 is not a superconductor above 0.47 K' (measured at 200 Oe, not 2 Oe); so superconductivity exists only in the pressure-processed (metastable, c-axis contracted) form; (2) the cycle 3 note's open rule question (does pressure annealing fall under the high-pressure exclusion?) is not answered by the rule text; the rule text, read literally, admits this sample. Read from the arXiv preprint, not the typeset JPSJ version.
reader_a.leads_for_library: Check the typeset JPSJ 84, 084703 (2015), Sec. 3.3, Fig. 4(b) and Fig. 6, against the arXiv text. Reports that ambient-synthesized Bi2OS2 does not superconduct (they support the current label for that form): Phelan et al., J. Am. Chem. Soc. 135, 5372 (2013), doi 10.1021/ja4011767 (abstract: 'Bi2OS2 ... is non-superconducting'); Shao et al., Supercond. Sci. Technol. 28, 015008 (2015), doi 10.1088/0953-2048/28/1/015008 (abstract: parent Bi2OS2 nonsuperconductive); Okada et al., Appl. Phys. Express 8, 023102 (2015), doi 10.7567/APEX.8.023102 (arXiv 1508.01654, read: undoped Bi2OS2 'did not show large diamagnetism above 2 K').

reader_b.paper_formula: Bi2OS2 (undoped; the paper also writes the family as Bi2(O,F)S2 = Bi(O,F)BiS2)
reader_b.at_pct_check: Bi2OS2 has 2+1+2 = 5 atoms. Bi 2/5 = 0.400, O 1/5 = 0.200, S 2/5 = 0.400. Row: Bi 0.400, O 0.200, S 0.400. Differences 0.000 on every element, within the 0.0015 limit. The paper's formula is the nominal composition; the actual composition of the high-pressure-annealed sample was not analysed.
reader_b.phase_or_sample: Polycrystalline bulk Bi2OS2, tetragonal P4/nmm (Fig. 4a). The superconducting samples are (i) ambient-synthesised Bi2OS2 that was then high-pressure annealed (2 GPa, 470 C, 1 h; a = 3.963(1) A, c = 13.794(3) A) and (ii) Bi2OS2 high-pressure synthesised from Bi2O3 + Bi2S3 (470 C, 2 GPa, 1 h; a = 3.964(2) A, c = 13.786(5) A; more impurity phases). XRD shows small amounts of Bi metal and Bi2S3 (and BN from the pressure medium); 'constituent phases were almost unchanged' by HP annealing. The as-synthesised ambient sample (a = 3.961(1) A, c = 13.808(2) A) is NOT superconducting above 0.47 K.
reader_b.page_table_or_figure: arXiv 1508.01656 (accepted version of J. Phys. Soc. Jpn. 84, 084703 (2015)): Sec. 3.3, pp. 4-5; Fig. 4(b) (ZFC magnetization of undoped Bi2OS2: as-synthesised, HP-annealed, HP-synthesised); Fig. 6 (Tc onset(mag) vs lattice parameters, undoped HP-annealed points near 1.8 K and 2.1 K); Sec. 4 and Conclusion.
reader_b.tc_criterion: Magnetization (ZFC, SQUID, 2 Oe): the authors give 'Tc of bulk superconductivity ... ~2 K' for the HP-annealed / HP-synthesised Bi2OS2. HP-annealed sample: diamagnetic onset ~4 K, kink in ZFC at 1.8 K with large diamagnetism below it; HP-synthesised sample: small diamagnetism from ~4 K, large diamagnetism below 2.1 K. Fig. 6 plots undoped high-pressure-sintered points at about 1.8 K and 2.1 K (read from the figure). The ~4 K onset is attributed by the authors to a minor impurity phase (probably Bi3O2S3), not to Bi2OS2.
reader_b.pressure: ambient during measurement (the paper: 'In HP annealing, high pressure is applied at high temperatures and physical properties are measured at ambient pressure.'). The superconducting samples were annealed or synthesised at 2 GPa, 470 C, 1 h before the measurement.
reader_b.measurement_method: Zero-field-cooled (and field-cooled for the HP-synthesised sample) dc magnetization, Quantum Design MPMS SQUID with iHelium3 insert down to 0.47 K; 2 Oe for the HP samples, 200 Oe for the as-synthesised sample. No ambient-pressure resistivity on undoped Bi2OS2 is shown.
reader_b.synthesis_conditions: Undoped Bi2OS2 by solid-state reaction at 300 C for ~100 h in an evacuated quartz ampoule with intermediate grindings; HP annealing of that product at 470 C, 2 GPa, 1 h in a cubic-anvil apparatus (BN pressure medium); separately, HP synthesis from Bi2O3 (99.9%) and Bi2S3 (99%) at 470 C, 2 GPa, 1 h.
reader_b.quote: These results suggest that the Tc of bulk superconductivity for the HP annealed / synthesized samples are ~2 K.
reader_b.evidence_note: Route STATED is met as the rule is written: the paper states bulk superconductivity, measured at ambient pressure, with Tc ~2 K, for a sample whose formula is exactly the row (Bi2OS2), and the authors attribute the bulk transition to Bi2OS2 (large diamagnetism, 4piM/H about -1.6 at 2 Oe in Fig. 4b; they also write 'In contrast, HP annealed Bi2OS2 showed superconductivity' and, in Sec. 4, 'in HP annealed / synthesized undoped Bi2OS2, superconductivity is achieved without intentional carrier doping'). Points the owner and sceptic should weigh: (1) superconductivity appears only after high-pressure annealing or high-pressure synthesis at 2 GPa; it is observed at ambient pressure, so the rule's exclusion 'superconductivity only under pressure' does not literally apply, but the earlier screen note flagged this as a rule question. (2) The same paper states that ambient-synthesised Bi2OS2 'is not a superconductor above 0.47 K' (Sec. 3.3, Fig. 4b, measured at 200 Oe), which is a verified null for that preparation and matches the current label for the ambient form. (3) Tc is approximate ('~2 K', the authors write 'suggest'); the ~4 K onset is assigned to an unidentified minor impurity not seen in XRD. (4) Composition is nominal; the samples contain small Bi and Bi2S3 impurities, neither of which superconducts at ambient pressure near 2 K. (5) I read the arXiv version; the published JPSJ text was not opened, but Crossref confirms the DOI, title and author list match.
reader_b.leads_for_library: Published version: T. Okada et al., J. Phys. Soc. Jpn. 84, 084703 (2015), doi:10.7566/JPSJ.84.084703, Sec. 3.3 and Figs. 4 and 6, to check the published wording matches arXiv 1508.01656. Ambient-pressure undoped Bi2OS2 (non-superconducting) is also in T. Okada et al., Appl. Phys. Express 8, 023102 (2015) and J. Shao et al., Supercond. Sci. Technol. 28, 015008 (2015), cited as refs. 17 and 18.

refutation_attempts: Source re-read: downloaded arXiv 1508.01656 (accepted version of JPSJ 84, 084703) and read the full text with pdftotext; viewed Fig. 4 (p. 12) and Fig. 6 (p. 14) as images. The readers' quotes are exact. Sec. 3.3: HP-annealed Bi2OS2 shows a diamagnetic onset ~4 K, a ZFC kink at 1.8 K and large diamagnetism below it; the HP-synthesised sample shows large diamagnetism below 2.1 K; the authors write the results 'suggest' bulk Tc ~2 K. Fig. 4(b): 4piM/H reaches about -1.6 (HP-annealed) and about -1.4 (HP-synthesised) at 0.47 K, 2 Oe, ZFC, not demagnetisation-corrected; FC in the inset is only about -0.02.

At.% arithmetic: Bi2OS2 = 5 atoms; Bi 2/5 = 0.400, O 1/5 = 0.200, S 2/5 = 0.400; row 0.400/0.200/0.400; difference 0.000 on each element. Holds, but the formula is nominal: the paper did not analyse the composition after the 2 GPa / 470 C treatment.

Bulk and pressure: polycrystalline bulk; magnetization measured at ambient pressure after processing at 2 GPa and 470 C (Sec. 1: 'physical properties are measured under ambient pressure'). The superconducting form exists only after high-pressure annealing or high-pressure synthesis; the same paper reports that Bi2OS2 made at ambient pressure is not a superconductor above 0.47 K (Sec. 3.3, Fig. 4b, 200 Oe).

Phase attribution: impurities are Bi metal, Bi2S3 and BN (Fig. 4a), none a superconductor near 2 K at ambient pressure; the ~4 K onset is assigned by the authors to an unidentified minor phase 'not seen in the XRD pattern'. The authors attribute the ~2 K bulk shielding to Bi2OS2 and Fig. 6 places the undoped HP points on the lattice-parameter trend of the F-doped samples. I found no evidence that the 2 K shielding belongs to another phase, but the sample does contain a superconducting phase the XRD did not identify, and no resistivity or specific heat on undoped Bi2OS2 is shown.

Replication and later reading: OpenAlex lists only 4 works citing the paper (Mizuguchi review JPSJ 88, 041001 (2019); Demura review NSM 2016; two high-pressure papers on other BiS2 compounds); none reproduces superconductivity in undoped Bi2OS2. The Mizuguchi 2019 review (arXiv 1808.05782, read), which cites this paper as ref. 39 under 'pressure effect' for Bi(O,F)BiS2, lists Bi2OS2 (BiOBiS2) with maximum Tc '-' in Table I and calls the parent phase a band insulator (Sec. 2.1). This is a secondary source, recorded as a lead, but it shows the field's own compilation did not adopt Bi2OS2 as a superconductor.

Where the table's zeros come from: three SuperCon zero reports for Bi2OS2 are consistent with the ambient-synthesised samples of Phelan et al. JACS 2013 (abstract: 'non-superconducting'), Shao et al. SuST 2015 (abstract: parent Bi2OS2 'nonsuperconductive') and Okada et al. APEX 2015 (read: no large diamagnetism above 2 K). These are real null measurements, not a data-entry error.

DOI check: FastTrack verify_reference (Crossref) confirms 10.7566/JPSJ.84.084703 is registered: 'Pressure Effects on Superconducting Properties of the BiS2-Based Superconductor Bi2(O,F)S2', J. Phys. Soc. Jpn. 84(8) 084703 (2015), 8 authors matching arXiv 1508.01656; no retraction flagged. The arXiv abstract page gives the same DOI.

contrary_reports.finding: Table I lists Bi2OS2 (BiOBiS2) maximum Tc as '-'; Sec. 2.1 calls the parent phase a band insulator. The review cites the task paper (ref. 39) but does not list undoped Bi2OS2 as a superconductor.

sceptic.evidence_note: Both readers read the paper correctly and quoted it exactly. The positive result is real as written, but it is for a metastable, pressure-processed form; the same paper and other primary papers verify that Bi2OS2 made at ambient pressure does not superconduct (down to 0.47 K here).

candidate_evidence_row_not_applied.phase_or_sample: Polycrystalline bulk, tetragonal P4/nmm; HP-annealed a = 3.963(1) A, c = 13.794(3) A; small Bi, Bi2S3, BN impurities; unidentified minor phase with onset ~4 K
candidate_evidence_row_not_applied.tc_criterion: ZFC magnetization kink at 2 Oe below which large diamagnetism appears (HP-annealed 1.8 K; HP-synthesised 2.1 K; authors: bulk Tc ~2 K)
candidate_evidence_row_not_applied.measurement_method: DC magnetization, SQUID (MPMS) with iHelium3 insert, ZFC 2 Oe

sceptic.verifier_reason: Do not apply. The arithmetic holds (Bi2OS2 = 0.400/0.200/0.400 exactly) and the paper does state bulk-like diamagnetic superconductivity near 2 K, measured at ambient pressure, in Bi2OS2 that had been annealed or synthesised at 2 GPa and 470 C. But there are reasons of substance to doubt that this composition, as a bulk sample at ambient pressure, is a superconductor in the sense of the table. (1) The same paper states that Bi2OS2 made at ambient pressure is not a superconductor above 0.47 K, and other primary reports (Okada APEX 2015, read: none above 2 K; Phelan JACS 2013 and Shao SuST 2015, abstracts) agree. The table's three zeros match these real null measurements, so the label is not a data error; superconductivity appears only in a metastable, strained, c-axis-contracted form made under high pressure. Whether such pressure-processed samples count was flagged in cycle 3 as an owner rule question to settle before relabelling, and RULES.md does not settle it. (2) The positive claim is a single unreplicated report: magnetization only (no resistivity or specific heat on undoped Bi2OS2), at 2 Oe, worded as 'suggest', with a superconducting impurity the XRD did not identify, and no analysis of composition after the high-pressure treatment of a band insulator that superconducts 'without intentional carrier doping'. No later paper reproduces it, and the field's 2019 review, which cites this paper, still lists Bi2OS2 with no Tc. Under 'when in doubt, do_not_apply', the label stays. If the owner rules that pressure-processed samples measured at ambient count, the candidate evidence row above (Tc 1.8 K, ZFC kink) is ready.

refutation_attempts: Re-read the primary abstract myself: OpenAlex get_work for DOI 10.1103/physrevb.50.13879 (record W1617699599) returned the full abstract. It names Lu2Ni3Si5, states superconductivity below 2.1 K (ac-susceptibility diamagnetic onset 2.1 K, resistive onset the same, zero resistance 2.0 K) and a specific-heat jump peaking at 1.9 K that the authors say indicates bulk superconducting ordering. SciSpace returned the same abstract text.

Composition arithmetic: Lu2Ni3Si5 has 2+3+5 = 10 atoms; Lu 2/10 = 0.2000, Ni 3/10 = 0.3000, Si 5/10 = 0.5000. Row Lu 0.200, Ni 0.300, Si 0.500. Difference 0.0000 on every element (limit 0.0015). Holds.

Bulk or film: the abstract describes a synthesised compound measured by resistivity, ac susceptibility and specific heat, with no film or nanostructure mentioned. The secondary source (arXiv 1409.1866, opened and read with pdftotext here) says the structure was probed on a powder sample. Bulk.

Impurity phase: the specific-heat jump has Delta Cp/(gamma Tc) = 1.1, against the BCS 1.43. If the transition came from a minor impurity, the jump normalised to the sample's gamma would be a small fraction of that; 1.1/1.43 is about 0.77, which fits a majority superconducting phase. Three probes agree on Tc to within 0.2 K. Lu2Fe3Si5 (6 K) cannot be the source because the sample has no Fe. I found no known Lu-Ni-Si or Ni-Si phase reported near 2 K in the searches run. Phase purity itself is not stated in the abstract.

Pressure: the abstract mentions no applied pressure or pressure cell; it reports routine low-temperature characterisation (resistivity 1.5-300 K, ac susceptibility 1.5-5 K, specific heat 1.7-30 K) of a newly reported superconductor. Ambient pressure is implied, not stated in words.

Structural doubt: the secondary source says that per this paper the powder structure could not be assigned unambiguously (orthorhombic Ibam, U2Co3Si5 type, with a possible slight monoclinic C2/c distortion). That concerns the structure type, not the composition or whether the sample superconducts.

The Crossref record shows no correction or retraction relation. The 2011 secondary source, written 17 years later, still calls Lu2Ni3Si5 superconducting with Tc = 2.1 K and says it is the only superconducting R2Ni3Si5 member.

Where the table's zeros may come from: not identified. The same group's series papers on R2Ni3Si5 (J. Appl. Phys. 75 (1994), DOI 10.1063/1.356709, Gd and Sm; IEEE Trans. Magn. 1994, DOI 10.1109/20.334279, Pr and Ho; J. Appl. Phys. 1997, DOI 10.1063/1.364666, magnetoresistance at 4.4 K) are about magnetic members and, by their abstracts, measured at 4.2-5 K or above, which could not see a 2.1 K transition. Ce2Ni3Si5 (PRB 46, 9009, 1992) was measured from 4.2 K. None of these is a measurement of Lu2Ni3Si5 below 2 K.

The Cava et al. 1994 abstract (same Bell Labs group) says Au-free LnPt2B2C could not be made single-phase and that Au substitution gives essentially single-phase material at the superstoichiometric composition LnPt1.5Au0.6B2C, which says nothing about phase purity at the stoichiometric x = 0.3 of the Carter sample. So the sample is superconducting in bulk at about 10 K, but whether the superconducting part has the row's composition (Au 5 at.%) or is an Au-poor LaPt2(+d)B2C phase with the gold in a second phase cannot be settled from what could be read.
reader_a.reason_if_not: Only the abstract of Carter et al. could be read; the paper is closed access and no arXiv or open copy exists (arXiv search found nothing). The abstract gives no phase purity, no synthesis, no Tc criterion and no statement on pressure. This matters here because Buchgeister et al. (1995) report that in nominal Ln(Pt,Au)2+dB2C samples the superconducting phase contains practically no gold (about LnPt2.1B2C), which, if true of the Carter sample, would make this a multi-phase sample whose superconducting part is another composition (5 at.% off in Au), an exclusion under the owner's rule. No bracketing series within 2 at.% was found.
reader_a.leads_for_library: 1) Carter, Batlogg, Cava, Krajewski, Peck, Takagi, Phys. Rev. B 50, 4216 (1994), DOI 10.1103/PhysRevB.50.4216: read the sample-preparation paragraph (arc melting, anneal, x-ray phase purity of the LaPt1.7Au0.3B2C sample), the C(T) figure near 10 K and how Tc was defined. 2) Cava et al., Physica C (1994), 'Stabilization of superconducting LnPt2B2C by partial substitution of gold for platinum', DOI 10.1016/0921-4534(94)90493-6: look for a table or figure of lattice parameters and Tc versus Au content for LaPt2-xAuxB2C (a Vegard shift would show Au incorporation) and any measured x = 0.2-0.4 samples that could bracket x = 0.3. 3) Buchgeister, Fuchs, Klosowski, Wiesner, Zawadzki, Physica C (1995), DOI 10.1016/0921-4534(95)00573-0: WDX table of the superconducting phase composition. 4) Michor et al., Phys. Rev. B (1995), 'Specific-heat analysis of rare-earth transition-metal borocarbides' (LaPt1.5Au0.5B2C), for comparison of sample quality.

reader_a.quote: Characteristics of superconductivity in Nb-Ti alloys (Nb-41-55 mass %Ti) are studied through electrical resistivity measurements.
reader_a.evidence_note: The named lead, Hulm & Blaugher 1961 (10.1103/physrev.123.1569), is paywalled. I could read only its abstract (FastTrack/OpenAlex record), and the abstract gives no Nb-Ti compositions or Tc values. As a replacement I read Takei 1984 in full (open access on J-STAGE, 5 pages). It is a single bulk Nb-Ti series of five specimens, all superconducting, with Tc decreasing monotonically with Ti. Its two specimens nearest the row sit at Nb 42.23 and 37.83 at.%, 2.23 and 2.17 at.% away, just outside the owner's 2 at.% bracket. I also read Hariharan et al. 1986 (Pramana 26, 513; 10.1007/BF02880911; ias.ac.in PDF) in full. Its alloys are Ti83, Ti73 and Ti65 (Nb 17, 27 and 35 at.%), with Tc 6.02, 7.43 and 8.97 K (50% resistance, Table 2). The nearest of these is 5 at.% from the row. I read abstracts only for the following. Wada, Tachikawa & Kato 1981 (IEEE Trans. Magn. 17, 61; 10.1109/TMAG.1981.1060925) studied 42 Ti-Nb-Hf alloys and says that in the as-rolled state the Tc of Ti-40at%Nb-3at%Hf is raised by about 0.3 K over Ti-40at%Nb alloy. Its Hc2(4.2 K) of 11.7 T for the Hf alloy is 0.4 T above that of Ti-40at%Nb, which implies a measured binary Ti-40at%Nb, i.e. this exact composition, with Tc above 4.2 K. The abstract gives no Tc number, and the full text is paywalled. Shapira & Neuringer 1965 report Tc = 9.0 K for Nb-56 at.% Ti (Nb 44 at.%), 4 at.% away. All of this is consistent with the row superconducting near 9-10 K, but nothing I read meets STATED or BRACKETED.
reader_a.reason_if_not: No source I could open states a Tc for Nb40Ti60 within 0.15 at.%. The best readable series (Takei 1984) brackets the row with superconducting specimens at 42.23 and 37.83 at.% Nb, which are 2.23 and 2.17 at.% away, so both miss the 2 at.% limit. The one paper that measured exactly Ti-40at%Nb (Wada et al. 1981) could be read only as an abstract, which gives no Tc value. Hulm & Blaugher 1961 is paywalled, and its abstract has no Nb-Ti data.
reader_a.leads_for_library: (1) Wada H., Tachikawa K., Kato T., 'Superconducting properties of Ti-Nb-Hf alloys', IEEE Trans. Magn. 17(1), 61-64 (1981), DOI 10.1109/TMAG.1981.1060925. Rev. 123, 1569 (1961), DOI 10.1103/physrev.123.1569: Ti-Nb Tc table. Takei's Fig. 3 reproduces Hulm points across about 34-49.5 mass% Ti, and an automated reading of that figure suggests one near 43.5 mass% Ti (about Nb 40.1 at.%); this is unverified. (1973): Tc versus composition for 22-38 at.% Nb, one side only. (6) Bychkov Yu.F., Herzog R., Khukhareva I.S., Cryogenics 21, 741 (1981): Nb-Ti Tc versus concentration.
